items.body: Listening to Crude Walnut Taste, it is tempting to focus on Giorgi Koberidze‘s compositional rigour: the electroacoustic transformations, the dialogue with Western classical forms, the microscopic attention paid to the behaviour of sound. Those elements are certainly there, but they risk obscuring something equally important. This is a remarkably funny album. After all, the opening track, “Horsing Around”, gives the game away immediately. Crude Walnut Taste is not funny in the sense of parody or quotation, but in the pleasure it takes in constantly wrong-footing the listener who might be expecting an academic work. A gesture suddenly changes direction, a rhythmic idea gathers momentum before being interrupted by an entirely different line of thought. Titles such as “Quasi Sonata-Allegro”, “Experimental, electro-accoustic, spatial audio, Georgian, sound design, Tbilisi, ambient – Adagio” and “Tbilisian Faux-Valse” gesture towards familiar classical forms, but only long enough for Koberidze to dismantle them. As the composer explains in the accompanying interview, these references belong to an earlier period of his practice, when his relationship with classical composition was more direct and, in his own words, more “primitive”. And this is the paradox at the heart of the album. On the one hand it sounds almost primitive, built from raw acoustic matter; on the other, the speed with which ideas appear, collide and disappear constantly propels it forward. Without resorting to the tired label of “retro-futurism”, the image that kept returning while I listened was Georgiy Daneliya’s Kin-dza-dza!. The 1986 Soviet science-fiction comedy follows two ordinary citizens transported to a distant galaxy where advanced civilisation appears to have regressed into something primitive. The film was, of course, scored by the late Georgian composer Giya Kancheli, yet there is a comparable measure of irony and lightness of touch running through both works. That playfulness extends to the sound world itself. Much of the album is constructed from recordings of the doli, the Georgian drum, chosen precisely because it carries no melodic baggage. Rather than treating the instrument as a symbol of national identity, Koberidze breaks it down into tiny fragments that become the raw material for an unexpectedly broad range of textures. The result is music that remains unmistakably physical. Even the electronics rarely transform those sounds outright. However, what remains most surprising, is the album’s speed, and not just its manic kinetic energy, but also the speed with which ideas appear only to mutate. Very little is allowed to settle. Musical thoughts collide with a kind of controlled frenzy that recalls someone thinking faster than they can speak. And yet, despite this restless surface, the music never feels erratic. It remains playful without becoming flippant, rigorous without turning solemn. That is a rare balance, and one that gives Crude Walnut Taste its distinctive character. To help us crack the walnut, we approached Giorgi Koberidze directly. Crude Walnut Taste began life as a 20-channel spatial work commissioned for MONOM’s 4D Sound system before being reimagined in stereo for this release. How did the process of translating such a physically immersive piece into a two-channel format affect your relationship to the material? Were there aspects of the original spatial architecture that had to be sacrificed, or did the reduction reveal new details that were previously hidden? I actually already knew how the piece would sound in stereo, because I don’t have a twenty-channel speaker setup at my studio. So while working on it, I was composing in stereo from the start, imagining what sound could fit where. We then spent two weeks at MONOM Studio in Berlin, where we had the chance to rearrange the piece, add things, and sometimes exclude things, but the core idea of the music was already written in stereo, and that’s what made it possible to translate the twenty-channel piece back down. Of course, a lot is lost in that reduction, but the core idea is still there. It works almost the same as watching an IMAX film in a normal movie theatre: whatever really matters stays in focus, stays at the centre. What the IMAX size gives you additionally is maybe more air, more space, something that isn’t crucial to understanding the film itself. I’d say it’s the same with this piece: what really matters is still there in stereo. The MONOM system just gives more space and some additional ideas, but I wouldn’t say the piece is focused only on those twenty channels. Generally, my belief is that good music can be played on a single-string guitar, even if it was written for a hundred-channel system, as long as the idea itself is strong, and as long as the music matters more than the form. If we’re not talking about a piece where form is more important than the music, then I think it’s easily translatable anywhere. Across Forests, Tales, Cities, Forests, its Epilogue, and now Crude Walnut Taste, the doli seems to occupy an increasingly central role in your work. On this album, the instrument is extensively sampled, dissected and reconstructed through micro-editing techniques. What drew you to the doli as the primary sonic source, and how did transforming it electronically alter your perception of an instrument so deeply embedded in Georgian musical culture? I use the doli because it has no pitch. My problem with using tonal instruments from the Caucasus – the duduk, say, or the chuniri – is that they come with already-written melodies and harmonies, and I find it very hard to know how to use that material in modern music. At some point I decided I would never touch existing melody or harmony, because it’s already there, it’s already enough. It doesn’t need anything from me, or from anyone, to be transformed. The doli is interesting because you can use it without ever touching a melody or a harmony, it gives you a lot of possibility to take micro-material from it instead. But anyone who understands sound and sound design knows that, basically, you can turn any sound into anything. The instrument you choose is just a source for material, and from there you can go anywhere; it’s really about what physical material you’re comfortable working with. In my case, it’s the doli simply because it’s here – you’re in Georgia, there are dolis everywhere, you can just grab one. Also, the quality of that sound already carries something very familiar to every Georgian. By using it, you’re lightly touching this historical heritage, but it doesn’t give you licence to overuse it – to base your music on something already precious to Georgians and then claim it as your own. Some people use old melodies, traditional melodies especially, and I’m not against using old pop music in modern work. But when it comes to traditional music, it’s more delicate. So even when we do use tonal instruments like the duduk, we’re very careful never to cross into an already-written melody from Georgian folk music. Earlier works such as Forests, Tales, Cities, Forests felt almost cartographic, mapping landscapes, memories and imagined geographies through graphic scores, ensembles and field recordings. Crude Walnut Taste seems more focused on texture, gesture and acoustic matter itself. Do you see this album as a departure from those narrative and spatial concerns, or as another way of exploring the relationship between place, memory and sound? Also, several track titles—”Tbilisian Faux-Valse”, “Quasi Sonata-Allegro”, “Experimental, electro-accoustic, spatial audio, Georgian, sound design, Tbilisi, ambient – Adagio”—appear to reference established musical forms, yet the music itself constantly undermines expectations through fragmentation, electroacoustic processing and playful subversion. To what extent are these titles intended as affectionate dialogues with classical traditions, and how important is humour or irony within your compositional practice? First, some context: Crude Walnut Taste was actually written much earlier than Forests, Tales, Cities, Forests – about five years earlier. What the two albums share is a certain playfulness with, and closeness to, classical music. In 2019, when I wrote Crude Walnut Taste, I was a much younger student of classical composition, so the way I integrated that knowledge into the album was more direct, less hidden, even a bit more “primitive” – the melodic and harmonic moments lean more overtly classical. That’s also where the track titles come from, which I actually chose later, closer to the album’s release: names like “Tbilisian Faux-Valse” or “Quasi Sonata-Allegro.” They’re not literal sonata-allegros or waltzes, of course, but the mood and the harmonic gestures really are drawn from there. Looking back, I wouldn’t use these references so directly today – in Forests, Tales, Cities, Forests, similar techniques are used much more hidden, on a deeper, more background level. So, from that perspective, this earlier album carries a bit of irony, a bit of humour, and that’s something I’m quite fond of. I’ve always wanted to find a way to put humour inside music – it’s genuinely hard to do. My friend and musical collaborator Luka, the other half of Awwwaea, always used to come up with wonderfully funny musical ideas; I was constantly amazed at how he could make our whole friend group laugh for hours over a single musical idea. I’d say this album carries a little of that same spirit. At the same time, it’s a very personal record. Even the title comes from childhood: crude walnut taste refers to eating very raw, unripe walnuts as kids – cracking them open with your fingers while they’re still green, watching your fingers turn green and then black from the juice. That taste takes me straight back to those childhood memories: sometimes fast, sometimes a little sad, but mostly very bright, full of colourful images and imagination – but still raw, because the sounds themselves are raw. After I finished the album, a friend told me at a small concert that it felt like “music made for sounds no one else is using.” I loved that description, because the sounds you hear really are raw – almost taken straight from the computer as they are, with very little additional sound design or processing layered on top. (Gianmarco Del Re)
items._genre: electroacoustic / experimental / contemporary classical / Georgian folk
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以格鲁吉亚传统打击乐器多里鼓为核心录音素材，将其拆解为微小碎片后通过电声手法进行变形与重组，形成丰富的声学纹理。作曲家频繁使用西方古典曲式名称如奏鸣曲快板、华尔兹等，却以戏谑方式在短时间内不断推翻这些引用，制造出持续出人意料的听觉体验。整体呈现出原始物质感与高速思维碰撞的张力——想法出现、碰撞、变异，却不流于杂乱。这是一部严肃却充满幽默感的作品，将民族乐器的物理性与当代电子技法融为一体，探索声音行为本身的微观逻辑。

items.body: 33 takes the traditional age of Christ at his death as the axis of a twelve-part electroacoustic cycle concerned with creation, incarnation, suffering, death and renewal. Yara Mekawei and Amir Rezk draw on biblical passages, Coptic Orthodox liturgy and Arabic recitation, but rarely allow the texts to remain intact: voices are repeated, stretched and submerged until scripture begins to function as rhythm and texture. Dense drones, fractured percussion, recitation and sudden clearings give the record a ceremonial character without turning it into devotional music. Its structure is particularly effective. “LOGOS” begins with John’s “In the beginning was the Word”; by “New Creation,” Revelation has replaced Genesis, with the first heaven and earth passing away and death itself disappearing. Between them, “Mysterion,” “33,” “Harrowing of Hades” and “Sackcloth Love” trace a passage through Eucharist, Crucifixion, descent and mourning. Musically, 33 sits between electroacoustic composition, dark ambient, and industrial electronics with a hint of prog rock, although none of those descriptions quite accounts for its restless construction. Mekawei and Rezk work with low drones, distorted orchestral sonorities, spoken voices, granular processing and percussion that repeatedly breaks apart just as it appears to settle into a pattern. The music can be oppressively dense, then abruptly hollowed out to expose a voice or a thin electronic residue. Rather than using electronics as accompaniment to the religious texts, the pair subject voice and instrumental material to the same processes: syllables become pulses, recitation turns into noise, and acoustic sounds lose their identifiable origins. This constant movement between intelligibility and abstraction gives the album much of its tension. What begins with a private anxiety surrounding the age of 33 expands into a work about mortality and transformation, with ancient texts treated not as historical artefacts but as material that can still be sounded, fractured and inhabited. To help us further navigate the album, we reached out directly to Yara Mekawei and Amir Rezk. 33 seems to follow an unusually coherent spiritual trajectory: from the Logos and creation in “LOGOS” and “Genesis,” through embodiment, suffering and death, to resurrection and finally the New Jerusalem in “New Creation.” Yet the album never feels like a straightforward retelling of scripture; texts are fragmented, repeated, obscured and absorbed into the electronics. Did you conceive the twelve tracks as a narrative or liturgical cycle from the outset, and how important was it that this progression could be felt without necessarily being understood literally? From the very beginning, we did not set out to create a straightforward textual retelling or a literal recitation of scripture. For us, the sacred texts are not static history; they are a living, sonic score. The progression across the twelve tracks was essential because we recognized that the trajectory of Christ’s life, from incarnation and embodiment, through suffering, descent, and ultimate renewal, is not merely a historical or theological timeline. It is a universal, spiritual archetype. It is a pattern that exists in the world and plays out in our own lives, in human endurance, migration, grief, and rebirth, whether we consciously recognize it or not. By weaving Yara’s personal story, her family inheritance, her grandmother’s warning, her lived experience of displacement and transformation, into this grander framework, the album becomes a dual narrative. The fragmentation, repetition, and electronic processing of the texts reflect how personal memory and sacred history actually operate in human consciousness: rarely as a clean, linear text, but as lingering textures, echoes, and internal pictures. It was crucial that a listener could feel this emotional and spiritual weight instinctively without needing to decipher every word literally, because the underlying trajectory of endurance and transformation is something universally felt in the human spirit. The number 33 begins from something intensely personal — a maternal warning about the thirty-third year of life — but the album gradually connects that age to Christ’s suffering, death and resurrection. In the title track especially, the language of Isaiah’s suffering servant and the Crucifixion seems to make personal vulnerability and sacred history overlap. How did that private association with the age of 33 become the organising principle of the record, and did making the album change what that number meant to you? The connection became obvious the moment we realized that 33 was not just a personal chronological marker, but the darkest point in Christ’s earthly life, the threshold of Gethsemane and the Cross, where He faced an unrepeatable cup of unknown suffering and abandonment. In our own human lives, those rock-bottom moments, where we carry an unbearable personal weight or face severe displacement, often become the precise pivots for profound transformation. The warning Yara inherited about the thirty-third year was essentially pointing toward this exact kind of personal Gethsemane: a room where you are tested to your limits, forcing a parallel between our lived vulnerability and what Christ endured. Creating 33 completely changed what that number means to us. Through the process of writing and immersing ourselves in these detailed sonic patterns and raw emotions, 33 transformed from an ominous, looming warning into a symbol of profound solidarity. It fixed a truth in our minds: our suffering in this life is never meaningless, nor is it carried in isolation. The Divine chose to step into human history and share directly in our exact grief, exile, and pain. Through making this record, the thirty-third year ceased to be a room of fear, becoming instead a reminder that we are never truly alone in the dark. Sacred language in 33 occupies a strange position between meaning and sound. Biblical passages, Coptic Orthodox material, Arabic and other vocal fragments can initially be intelligible, but repetition and electronic processing often push them toward rhythm, texture or something resembling incantation. Yara, your previous work has already explored ways of translating sacred texts into sonic structures; how did the two of you approach the voice here? Were you interested in preserving the theological meaning of these texts, or in reaching a point where the sound of devotion itself becomes the compositional material? For us, it was never a choice between preserving theological meaning or turning the text into pure abstraction, we wanted both. We approached the sacred texts as both a coherent narrative framework and a stream of subconscious thought, treating the voice as a primary musical texture. We deeply respect the inherent power of music to imprint a specific fingerprint upon the mind and the soul. However, we wouldn’t use the word “incantation” to describe this process. Instead, we see the voice and its electronic transformations as a sonic blessing carried through the physical sound waves themselves. We knew that many people listening across the world wouldn’t understand Arabic or Coptic, but we believed that sound itself can transcend language barriers. By layering, repeating, and processing these sacred fragments, we wanted to carry the spiritual energy and raw devotion directly to the listener’s intuition. The theological meaning grounds the structure, while the sonic vibration allows the blessing to reach anyone who listens, regardless of whether they can translate the words. There is a striking circularity between the beginning and end of the album. “LOGOS” opens with John’s “In the beginning was the Word,” while “New Creation” ultimately arrives at Revelation’s vision of the first heaven and earth passing away, God wiping away every tear, and death ceasing to exist. Between those points, the music moves through creation, the body, Eucharist, suffering, mourning and resurrection. Do you think of 33 as moving from one creation to another — and, if so, is “new creation” primarily a Christian theological idea for you, or does it also describe a personal process of destruction and transformation that took place while making the record? It is deeply both: a personal process of transformation and a theological truth made manifest. On a personal and artistic level, 33 is our very first collaboration together, so the album itself is literally a “new creation” born from our two individual musical worlds. We share the belief that marrying the arts with the sacred is like bringing heaven and earth together, much like the Incarnation of the Divine Logos coming down to breathe new life into His creation and bloom into a new Tree of Life. J.R.R. Tolkien spoke of artists as “sub-creators” or co-creators alongside the Great Creator. By deliberately inviting the Divine into our sound, making a “new creation” was never about trying to invent a new genre of music; it was about marrying the eternal with the earthly, which makes the work spiritual and new at its core. Making this album was an essential process of bringing light directly into the desolation of our own personal suffering and “stations” of life. It was a way to ground those difficult experiences in hope and meaning, not just for ourselves, but hopefully for anyone who listens to the record. (Gianmarco Del Re)
items._genre: electroacoustic / dark ambient / industrial electronics / experimental
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以基督受难年龄33岁为轴，构建了一个十二部分的电声循环，主题涵盖创世、道成肉身、受难、死亡与重生。创作素材取自圣经段落、科普特正教礼仪与阿拉伯语诵读，但文本被反复重复、拉长、淹没，直到经文本身转化为节奏与音色。专辑坐落于电声作曲、暗氛围与工业电子之间，低频嗡鸣、扭曲的管弦音色、颗粒化处理与不断碎裂的打击乐交织，构筑出仪式感而非纯粹的虔敬音乐。结构上从《约翰福音》的"太初有道"出发，经圣餐、十字架、下冥府与哀悼，最终抵达《启示录》的新天新地。声音设计将人声与器乐材料置于同一处理逻辑下：音节化为脉冲，诵读化为噪音，声响失去可辨来源，始终在可懂与抽象之间游移。这件作品将私人焦虑扩展为对死亡与转化的凝视，让古老文本成为仍可被碎裂、栖居的活性物质。

items.body: The Getaway could easily have stood on its own, but the remix sequence expands its central idea: fractured industrial sound behaving almost like an alien transmission, constantly mutating through minute edits, glitches, and rhythmic interference. Chiseled from front to back with remarkable precision The Getaway by Unterm Rad   Mike Slansky, operating as Unterm Rad, continues his run of punishing industrial IDM with The Getaway for the ever-consistent Bulgaria-based Mahorka imprint. With a background spanning audio engineering, expansive sound design, and graphic work reaching back to the Tympanik Audio era, Slansky was also a key component of the now-shuttered Point Source Electronic Arts collective. His work has long occupied darker electronic spaces, and The Getaway pushes further into that territory through an unusually constrained process: the album was composed entirely from short instrument clips and sounds supplied through Point Source’s Genome sample kits, each fragment carefully edited, processed, and sequenced until it evolved into something entirely new. No synthesizers, AI, or outside sound sources were used, adhering to the open-source spirit of the Genome project. Seven original pieces emerge as dark-grey slabs of machinery, where microscopic edits and fractured rhythms give each track a strangely extraterrestrial charge. Up front, “Hang Me Out To Dry” drives through minimal industrial fissures with a beat-heavy barrage of rugged technoid tones, metallic grit, and tightly controlled distortion. “They’re On To Us” narrows the focus further, exposing Slansky’s precision-built rhythmic glitches as tiny mechanical movements seem to twitch beneath the surface, while “Cornered” opens into broken beats and cavernous echoes, giving the record a sense of mechanical engineer​ing operating somewhere far beyond human reach. Transparent details become increasingly exposed :: The final six pieces hand Slansky’s material over to Access to Arasaka, Evaluation Copy, Vaag, Feederwire, Hexalyne, and Cole, each pulling the source tracks into a distinct interpretation. Rather than simply extending the album, these remixes reveal just how much microscopic movement exists inside Slansky’s sound structures. Access to Arasaka and Hexalyne sharpen the material into brisk, erratic sci-fi electro-nics; Evaluation Copy scorches through beats and bass; Vaag bends the rhythms into flexible broken beat contortions; and Feederwire drags everything through piercing industrial low-end vibrations. Cole’s closing interpretation is perhaps the most surreal, stripping the machinery back until its strange, transparent details become increasingly exposed. The Getaway could easily have stood on its own, but the remix sequence expands its central idea: fractured industrial sound behaving almost like an alien transmission, constantly mutating through minute edits, glitches, and rhythmic interference. Closing with “The Walls Are Closing In,” before the remixes kick in, Slansky lets pressure evaporate into sparse technoid shifts, leaving behind an album that feels both rigorously engineered and strangely alive. By opening his source material to collaborators, he turns a tightly controlled sonic experiment into a broader study of industrial texture, glitch mechanics, and extraterrestrial electronics—chiseled from front to back with remarkable precision. The Getaway is available on Mahorka. [Bandcamp] The Getaway by Unterm RadThe post Unterm Rad :: The Getaway (Mahorka) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.
items._cn_summary: Unterm Rad（Mike Slansky）的专辑完全由Genome采样包中的短小乐器片段和声音构成，经碎片化编辑、处理与序列编排后演变为全新的机械声响，全程未使用合成器、AI或外部音源。这种极度克制的制作方式产出七首深灰色调的工业IDM曲目，以微观级的剪辑与断裂节奏营造出类外星的电荷感。专辑后半段将素材交由Access to Arasaka、Evaluation Copy等六位艺术家进行重混，各自将原始音轨推向不同方向——电音化、破碎节拍扭曲、低频共振乃至细节剥离。这些重混不仅延伸了专辑，更揭示了Slansky声音结构内部存在的微观运动层次。整张专辑围绕裂缝化的工业声响这一核心概念展开，呈现出持续变异、近似异星信号的听觉体验。

items.body: It has been about four years since the Brazilian act Aesthetische released their last full-length album, but in the meantime, Gui Pires and Fab Viscardi have kept us entertained with an annual EP. “Every Beat Matters” serves as a metaphor for everything we can do to fight injustice, fascism, prejudice, war, and more. Musically, this translates into four brand-new tracks followed by three remixes. Aesthetische return to their roots more than ever, recalling their former project, Aghast View, with a sound deeply rooted in EBM. It is a meticulously crafted production boasting rich soundscapes and razor-sharp basslines that once again bring Front Line Assembly to mind. The tracks are driven by stomping beats that give them maximum club appeal. To my ears, the first three tracks all sound like potential singles, although Aesthetische clearly have a soft spot for “Chew The Loop,” which appears in three additional and strong remixes. The vocals round everything out, complemented by well-placed samples. One track remains instrumental, yet sounds incredibly effective. Aesthetische never disappoint, but this new EP is undoubtedly one of their strongest releases to date. It represents intelligent, impactful EBM. (Rating:9). Side-Line reported the release of “Every Beat Matters” on June 26, 2026 via Alfa Matrix. Listen to “Chew The Loop”’: Chew The Loop by Aesthetische About Aesthetische Aesthetische is a Brazilian EBM/industrial duo formed by Gui Pires and Fab Viscardi in 2012. Both musicians were previously known for their work in Aghast View and Biopsy, one of Brazil’s pioneering electro-industrial acts of the 1990s. After Aghast View, the duo launched Aesthetische as a new vehicle for modern EBM fused with trance, techno-body music, and industrial atmospheres. The band signed with Belgian label Alfa Matrix in 2012 and has since maintained an exclusive release partnership with them, issuing a steady discography of albums, EPs, and digital singles across physical and digital formats. Albums “Powerswitch” (2012, Alfa Matrix) – Issued in multiple editions, including a box version. “HybridCore” (2014, Alfa Matrix) – A follow-up blending hard-hitting EBM with more melodic synth textures. “Co3xist3ns3” (2019, Alfa Matrix) – Marked a return after several years, further exploring hybridized EBM and trance. “Rvprty” (2022, Alfa Matrix AM 3400DJ) – A digital-only release containing ten tracks. Singles & EPs “Nachtbrenner” (2013, Alfa Matrix) “Statement / Amplitude Zero” (2013, Alfa Matrix) “Colder Lights EP” (2014, Alfa Matrix) “Dirt And Basslines” (2015, Alfa Matrix) “Cold Is Clean” (2015, Alfa Matrix) “We Follow Blindly” (2016, Alfa Matrix) “In My Aurora” (2017, Alfa Matrix) – Featuring Noemi Aurora on vocals. “MMXX” (2020, Alfa Matrix) “Overflow” (2021, Alfa Matrix) “Boiling Over EP” (2023, Alfa Matrix) “Confidence Is Silent” (2024, Alfa Matrix) Split EP “4.4U [2012.11]” (2012, Alfa Matrix) – Digital compilation shared with Metroland, Mentallo & The Fixer, and Daniel B. Prothèse. Alfa Matrix has continued the pace since, following “Boiling Over” (2023) with “Confidence Is Silent” (2024), “Selling Fear” (2025) and now “Every Beat Matters” in 2026.

items.excerpt: An obsession, exaggeration Lust, desire and adoration Lose yourself in someone else Limerence closes every door Robots In Love have the sort of name that promises chrome-plated heartbreak, and their latest single Cease and Desist delivers an emotional sucker punch. items.body: An obsession, exaggeration Lust, desire and adoration Lose yourself in someone else Limerence closes every door Robots In Love have the sort of name that promises chrome-plated heartbreak, and their latest single Cease and Desist delivers an emotional sucker punch. The New Zealand dark electronic duo of vocalist-producer Elenor Rayner and drummer-producer Alex Burchell builds the song around obsession gone feral: attraction narrowing into fixation, fixation hardening into dependency, and reason getting shoved somewhere beneath the furniture. There is no polite exit once the appetite starts feeding on itself. The guitars come down hard, with hardcore licks driven right up against industrial metal without quite falling into Ministry cosplay. There is some of SINE’s bruising electronic pressure here, along with the blackened mechanical weight of latter-day Gary Numan, while the bigger synth architecture brushes against HEALTH, Nine Inch Nails, Sirus, and V.A.S.T. Burchell’s drumming has the clipped exactitude of somebody who has spent years learning how machines think, while Rayner sings from inside the mess those machines could never clean up. Desire behaves like bad wiring in the skull, making sleeplessness feel necessary and self-erasure almost reasonable. The chorus grows huge enough to suggest somebody shouting through concrete, yet the verses keep dragging the listener back toward the private humiliation of knowing exactly what is happening and remaining unable to stop it. “I recently discovered the word ‘limerence’ and started thinking about extreme obsession,” says Rayner. “Hence the line “limerence closes every door” where no amount of reasoning can get through. Musically, it’s got dark, heavy riffs, cinematic synths and an epic chorus.” The video, directed by Lichen Sorrel and Rayner, places the band inside a rain-soaked environment where reality keeps slipping sideways. Their movements feel slowed and strangely detached, as though the performers have wandered into somebody else’s private hallucination and decided to finish the set anyway. Watch the video for Cease and Desist below: Rayner has been working toward this collision for decades. She began playing Australian pubs on bass at fourteen before moving into electronic production on an Atari computer, “which opened up a universe of creating sounds and moulding them into rhythms and melodies until they evoke the exact feeling I need.” Her history runs through Soulscraper, Sobriquet, Snog, and The Crystalline Effect before Robots In Love took shape in New Zealand in 2017. Joined by Burchell in this current powerhouse incarnation, the project has developed a nasty elegance that can turn technical precision into emotional damage. With second album OVERRIDE ahead and guitarist Henry Flynn Wall joining the record, Cease and Desist makes obsession feel less romantic than chemical, compulsive, and absurd in the terrible way our worst impulses often are. Love may open doors, but limerence bolts them shut from the inside. Listen to Cease and Desist below and pre-order OVERRIDE here. items._cn_summary: 新西兰双人组合Robots In Love以单曲《Cease and Desist》呈现了一次关于执念失控的声学解构。主唱兼制作人Elenor Rayner与鼓手Alex Burchell将硬核吉他切线与工业金属质感并置，合成器架构层叠构建出沉重的机械压力，鼓点精准如机器运算。歌曲以"limerence"（痴迷状态）为核心意象，描绘吸引力如何异化为依赖、理性如何被吞噬——副歌如穿过混凝土的呐喊，verse段落却将听者拖回清醒的自知之痛。Rayner早年在Atari电脑上探索声音塑形的经历贯穿其创作脉络，从澳洲pub巡演到暗潮电子领域，最终在新西兰形成这一兼具技术精度与情感破坏力的项目。第二张专辑《OVERRIDE》即将到来，吉他手Henry Flynn Wall加入使声音更具侵略性，将执念演绎为化学式的强迫与荒诞，而非浪漫化的情感。

items.body: Oh how I want to love you Oh how I love to want you Oh how I love to hate you Oh how I hate to love you A persuasive EBM bassline can make almost any terrible proposition sound like it’s worth considering. Charm School’s Desolation makes the most of that weakness, setting a romance of taunts, submission, and calculated cruelty to a groove with suspiciously good manners. The invitation is easy to accept; the lyrics give you every reason to reconsider. The single pairs the Louisville-rooted, Los Angeles-based project with Matia Simovich of INHALT, who wrote the music, while Andrew Sellers, aka Andrew Charm, supplied the vocals and lyrics. It also serves as the lead single from a forthcoming EP that will include the late Steve Albini’s mix of Simulacra, Charm School’s first single. Matia Simovich of INHALT Simovich opens proceedings with a funky synth bassline, setting old-school synth stabs against drums intent on keeping the floor occupied. Metallic synth accents add a peculiar mechanical funk, their hard surfaces catching against the low end’s easy movement. There’s an EBM discipline to the arrangement and an Italo appetite for pleasure, with a trace of darkwave unease making itself comfortable between the two. Every sharp edge has something supple moving around it. Sellers attacks the vocal with a Stooges-era Iggy Pop drawl, mixed with the timbre and cadence of Lou Reed at his most forceful onstage. The compressed vocal sits prominently in the mix, with reverb sending the words ricocheting as though they were bouncing off sheet steel or passing through the blades of an industrial fan. That peculiar treatment gives each phrase a cold metallic afterimage. As the vocal develops, a bubbling synth figure lifts the groove, lending a playful buoyancy to a song whose romantic prospects are deteriorating by the line. The opening verse treats manipulation as a sales pitch, with a lover boasting of their dishonesty while angling to become the sole object of another person’s belief. By the second verse, that desire for control has tipped into a plea for surrender, even deception, as though being consumed by someone might offer its own peculiar relief. The roles seem to trade places, with domination and dependence feeding the same appetite. Images of kneeling, worship, and bodily sacrifice push the devotion toward something frighteningly absolute. The repeated title leaves that exchange with a bleak destination, while the closing permutations of wanting, loving, and hating keep rearranging the terms without resolving them. Each small change shifts the emotional balance. Pleasure survives in the music even as the words describe a relationship consuming itself, and the bassline keeps making its persuasive case for staying another few minutes. The collaboration also extends a connection dating back to our 2023 coverage of Simulacra, which credited Simovich with drum programming and noted alternate mixes by both Simovich and Albini. The forthcoming EP brings Albini’s version into the release plans alongside this new material, linking Charm School’s first statement to their latest electronic excursion. Listen to Desolation below and order the single here. Desolation by Charm School Sellers formed Charm School with longtime collaborators Matt Filip and Drew English, drawing on a Louisville upbringing steeped in Slint, Crain, and Rodan, alongside the catalogs of Touch & Go and Drag City. The disruptive instincts of PiL, Swell Maps, and The Fall sit beside an affection for Fugazi and Nation of Ulysses. Their debut EP, Finite Jest, appeared in July 2023, followed by the broader musical reach and acerbic satire of January 2025’s Debt Forever. This February’s Schadenfreude Ploy continued their examination of manipulation, tech wealth, and artificial intelligence. On Desolation, that interest in power finds an intimate setting, with two people apparently quite prepared to make each other miserable. Charm School will join Dildox for dates in Louisville and Knoxville before returning to Los Angeles for Oblivion in October. items.body:
Curating a retrospective of 40 years of recorded music is a daunting task, particularly when it is your own. Accurately representing the arc of the work and the life that created it requires frankness and acceptance. It is a process punctuated with winces and sighs and the occasional grin. Composer and improviser Jin Hi Kim experienced it all when compiling The Jin Hi Kim Collection, recently issued by Neuma. If the use of “odyssey” requires a great voyage, discovering new lands, and encountering titans, then Kim’s journey easily qualifies. Not only did she leave Korea at 23 for the US in 1980, Kim traversed an arguably greater gulf by leaving her elite training in traditional Korean music to study electronic music and composition with Lou Harrison, Terry Riley, and others. In the intervening decades, she worked with leading exponents of contemporary composition and improvisation like Kronos Quartet and Derek Bailey, and transformed the komungo, the traditional five-foot-long lute dating from the 4th Century CE, exponentially extending its sonic range through computer interfaces and signal processing.

Rediscovery accompanied the selection process for the 9-CD Collection. She was especially surprised when reviewing early works transliterating Korean music through Western instruments, or employing graphic notation. “It was created by a young mind,” Kim recently recalled with a laugh. “Sometimes it was hard to hear that’s what I did. But it was also good evidence for an archival collection. It was a wonderful feeling to look at everything I did – well, almost everything – but one thing that I was really proud about it is that there is not just one kind of music. Each piece has its Korean roots but, like I’ve said, I came to America to make new music, so I look at my 40 years of work and, yeah, I achieved that. So, it was a very satisfying process.

“When I listen to some of the improvisations, I realized how young and unafraid I was. Komungo has a limited sound compared to other instruments. When you work with virtuoso improvisers, they have vocabularies that are so rich. They are creating so many different colors and textures, but komungo has limits. It doesn’t allow you to express so much of the story. It has a meditative energy, of nothingness, of slowness. I was so brave to use this instrument with such incredible masters and to communicate with them and create music with them. I did it somehow with my inner energy. I was able to present this inner energy.”

The Collection almost equally divides Kim’s work in composition and improvisation, with five discs devoted to works for orchestra and chamber music ensembles, and four documenting improvisations with, among others, an impressive diversity of percussionists, including Gerry Hemingway, Susie Ibarra, and Tony Oxley, and string players like Bill Frisell, Min Xiao-Fen, and Hans Reichel. If anything can be read into it, the slight tilt reflects her ardent pursuit to articulate the concept of Living Tones Compositions, and how central it is to her work.

“The most important thing about the Living Tones Compositions is to convey the Korean element and philosophy through Western contemporary music,” she explained. “When I came to the United States after training in traditional Korean music, European classical music was more respected in Korea than the traditional music. They didn’t know much about American avant-garde music then, in the 1970s. I was a young musician who trained with the very best teachers and saw that I was not respected because I was not doing Western music.

“That created within me a great desire to fix that problem. You can’t fix anything, but I was young, I had a passion and a mission. I was living in the United States; I was composing for Western musicians; so how could I make this Korean idea, this Korean state of mind in making music, how could I put this together with Western music with equal respect? That was my thing. All my Living Tones Compositions come from the idea of putting together the Korean context and philosophy and Western instruments and musical context, to see how Western musicians took to the Korean attitude – not necessarily techniques, scales, anything like that – but this attitude, this state of mind. That’s what I’m doing with Living Tones music.

“Korean traditional music was once influenced by Chinese music,” Kim prefaced to explain the context and philosophy of Korean music, which she also detailed extensively in her book, Duality of Ancient Korean Roots and Western New Music. “Korean music can be divided into folk music and court music. Court music was quite different from music of ordinary people. The court was deeply influenced by ancient Chinese philosophy – yin and yang; the five elements, and ancient ancestors worship. The music wasn’t entertainment; it was ritual – that was part of both court and folk music. For ordinary people, they associated music with the shaman. For court music, there were virtuoso musicians who created an austere music, based on a philosophy of cosmic sound and abstract thinking; but for ordinary people, the shaman always took care of pain, community pain. Music was performed for celebrations of harvests and other things, but more for problems like drought, someone who is sick, some kind of problem. The shaman is always dealing with the problem of pain in their lives. They always had to sing something very sad. Her song has nothing to do with joyous things – always grief and pain. Ordinary people related to that.

“Both court and folk music had an emphasis on energy – they never thought of music as just sound. It had healing energy. In the folk community, they tried to imitate the shaman, the way she sang, shaking the notes, trying to reach out to another spirit, trying to connect heaven and earth. If you listen to a shaman’s song, there’s a very strong vibrato. The instrumentalists who don’t sing listen to this type of music; it’s very touching, very soulful, and it reflects the problems in their lives. Korean instrumentalists are all shaking, shaking their hands, shaking their instruments, shaking their notes. I play komungo, where the strings can move a lot, up and down, so you can really shake the notes and express the music in the same way as the shaman. I translate that process, that context, that spirit, into Living Tones. Each tone has its own light, and because it has its own light, its time is elastic. It is not like abstract Western time, where you count the time of each note perfectly, and you don’t have the space for microtones. There’s no time to do that in Western music. Time becomes much more open and that’s why in Korean music they don’t talk about abstract time but time in a cycle. Within that cycle, you have a lot of freedom of how to use that space with deep vibratos or any other articulation to create that intense feeling.”

The qualities Kim ascribes to Korean music are manifest in the komungo. It has a palpably plangent sound, with a bass register lower and more resonant than the guembri’s and the sting of ancient harps in its highest notes. It has a timbral luster comparable to the dark, iridescent glazes of pit-fired ceramics or the blocks of deep color that hover over the black basecoats of a Mark Rothko painting. Its dredge-like twang and the skeletal figures central to the music stop the racing, associative Western mind dead in its tracks. Even before Kim augmented the instrument with signal processing, Western improvisers had a strong attraction to the komungo. Conversely, improvisation has, over the decades, impacted Kim’s outlook.

However, Kim has a nuanced view on how improvisation has influenced her. “Influence is the result over a long period,” she elaborated, “because I played with a person one time or two times. That long period is a really deep space. It’s not that a particular musician gave me something. It is that the experience of playing with someone becomes part of my life experience. Now I look at something differently than when I was young. I understand how the universe works because of scientists and I understand how improvisation works because of improvisers. When you travel all around the world – I’ve performed in over 60 countries and have lived in some of these countries for a long time, six months or even a year – then you have an incredibly different life perspective. All of those things interest me. So, I have been influenced by many things over the decades, so that when I play with someone, it is not just that moment I am responding to; it’s everything about the other musicians: their instruments; their traditions; their culture. That gives me a very clear idea what to do.

“When I was young, I was so desperate to communicate successfully with each improviser I played with. I was trying to understand their personality; I was trying to understand their vocabulary. There have been very few times that I played on the spot without any information about the people I was playing with. I had heard them before I had the opportunity to play with them, playing with other musicians or solo. In my own way, I understood who they are. If I don’t understand them and their musical elements, I have no way to contribute anything on komungo. I have to understand their personality, their energy, how they process the music. Not all people process the same way; some people are poetic; some people are very emotional; some people are very funny. Everybody has those things happening. Understanding that was very important to me. It helped me to communicate, to hear what they were giving me, so I could give back. I listened a lot to what they were doing at a particular moment.”

Given that improvisers spanning James Newton and Elliott Sharp, and Rüdiger Carl and Oliver Lake, are heard throughout the box set, it is noteworthy that Kim singles one out to illustrate her approach to improvisation. “When I work with William Parker, he has a very deep energy in his soul,” she said of the bassist. “When I played with him, he influenced me with his deep energy. It’s really big. That influenced me to be really big. That bigness, that abundance, that tireless energy; that lets us play a really long time. He has the qualities to do something that a Korean shaman could do, playing the same idea over and over and over for a long time – trance like – but the energy becomes more powerful. William Parker has that type of energy. The bass is like the komungo; it has a deep energy and incredible power. I’m really influenced by that.”

Retrospectives like the Collection are generally considered to be merely summations, but in Kim’s case, it is more a marker of distance travelled and journeys ahead. “It reflects my continuous evolution as an artist. Throughout my musical journey, I have always searched for new ways to express myself creatively while remaining deeply rooted in my Korean musical identity.

“In essence, every work in this collection is the result of my enduring desire to elevate often-neglected Korean aesthetics, shaped alongside the freedom I found in America – a place that allowed me to pursue my artistic passions and ideas without limitation.

“Today, my perspective extends beyond national boundaries to the increasingly interconnected global community. I have aspired to use music as a spiritual and transformative force to confront social challenges. I believe this has become the new direction of my artistic journey.”

Kim’s new direction has steered her towards to uplifting marginalized subalterns and breaking through the fourth wall of the concert hall separating musicians from listeners. “Right now, because the world has changed so much, and America is now so blue, and so many people are mentally ill – I know because I recently gave a music meditation workshop at the Yale mental health center – I want to do something about community pain. I always go back to what the shaman does. I think I have sort of achieved my goal of blending Korean and Western ways of thinking with Living Tones, so right now I want to make music that the community participates in. Not necessarily well-trained musicians, but anybody who is interested. I already started on this in 2023 with a piece called ‘Ritual for Earth.’ I would like to do these things for now. I’m not anxious about my career or my next commission. I’m thinking about community pain, environmental issues like wildfires and floods, the world we are living in. So, if I have the opportunity, working with communities is what I want to do.”

items.body:
The brotherhood of foundational European avant garde bassists gets smaller with each passing year. And among those still living, some are either inactive for various reasons or working in other fields, musical or otherwise. So, the subset of ones still going is a small but precious list.

Among them is the Netherlands’ Arjen Gorter. Ask even a relatively informed listener of European avant garde jazz about him and almost invariably the first association will be Willem Breuker, and more specifically his Kollektief. Gorter did anchor that group for the entirety of its existence (1975-2010, with a retrospective farewell tour coming after Breuker’s death) alongside drummer Rob Verdurmen, allowing Breuker and a rotating cast of string and horn players (though trombonist Bernard Hunnekink was another stalwart) to navigate complex and subversive music, confident that a strong foundation would always support them. But like Jimmy Cobb always being referenced first and sometimes only as the last living participant of Kind of Blue after Miles Davis died in 1991, Gorter’s career, still ongoing, is hardly exclusive to his work with Breuker.

Gorter was born in Amsterdam on January 2nd, 1948 and he has resided in the Dutch capital his whole life. His road to the bass was a circuitous one. As he wrote in an email, “I liked the accordion when I was very young. It was common in the Amsterdam streets of the ‘50s, but the tunes that my teacher made me play were too silly, so that did not last. My dad imported musical instruments. He brought a slightly damaged ukulele home and so at around 11 I tried playing along with the nightly jazz broadcasts on French and Belgian radio. The father of a friend had a small jazz collection and I loved the Art Blakey Blue Note 45s, the Monk LP and the other stuff he had. So that ukulele was replaced by a guitar. I started jamming in our attic with friends and others and at some point someone brought a double bass upstairs and left it there for six months. I had fun playing it and managed to buy it from him once he showed up again.”

During high school Gorter played guitar in a band for school dances, repertoire ranging from period rock tunes to jazz compositions. He began college in 1966, aiming to study political science and sociology, the same year he first worked professionally with Breuker, having heard the older reed player’s bands around town and once playing with him at a jam session. Gorter was invited to join a new Breuker group, which performed at the Loosdrecht Jazz Competition as a sextet, then expanded to almost two-dozen musicians for the final stage. This group would make Litany for the 14th of June 1966 (Relax) in late October 1966, Gorter’s recording debut alongside two other bassists, the much older Dick van der Capellen and Victor Kaihatu.

Gorter would balance university and performing for a few years. During this time, he would work with Germany’s Gunter Hampel, appearing on his April 1968 Wergo date Gunter Hampel Group + Jeanne Lee and participating in the November 1968 Total Music Meeting in Berlin, where photo evidence has him in a bizarre encounter with Hampel, John McLaughlin, Sonny Sharrock, Pharoah Sanders, Roy Ayers, Laurie Allan, and Roel Kroes. 1969 saw even more activity: more Hampel work, including the album The 8th of July 1969 (inaugurating his Birth imprint); playing on German trumpeter Manfred Schoof’s FMP release European Echoes and being part of the Peter Brötzmann Oktett at the International Holy Hill Jazz Meeting (alongside Buschi Niebergall and Peter Kowald; Richard Williams’ review of European Echoes in the March 14th, 1970 issue of Melody Maker saying, “It’s an astonishingly powerful performance, with particularly superb work by Dudek, Bailey and the three basses, who play a really fantastic trio section.”). Gorter is also heard on the Live at The Bohemia Jazzclub recording by Hans Dulfer’s Soulbrass Inc., as well as a track with Breuker and Han and Peter Bennink heard on the Instant Composers Pool cheese box. As Gorter recalled, “I managed to juggle both activities until the end of 1969, but I was more on the road than in Amsterdam and had to make a choice and I chose the activity that gave me way more satisfaction.”

During the first half of the ‘70s, Gorter and Breuker did not work together often, at least as can be gleaned from available recordings: Hampel’s People Symphony (Birth, 1970) and part of his group that participated in German avant garde composer Hans Werner Henze’s Der Langwierige Weg In Die Wohnung Der Natascha Ungeheuer; and an unofficial Amsterdam recording from 1973 under Breuker’s leadership and a live date from Leo Cuypers in 1974, both with groups prefiguring the Kollektief (Cuypers was its first pianist). Otherwise Gorter was busy – again, at least on record – with Hans Dulfer, Kees Hazevoet, Theo Loevendie, Alexander Von Schlippenbach, and the Irène Schweizer-Rüdiger Carl Quartet. The latter two were significant. Gorter was part of the second iteration of Schlippenbach’s Globe Unity Orchestra, Niebergall and Kowald in tow once more (a 1970 Berlin Jazz Festival performance released in 2001) and the Schweizer-Rüdiger Carl group that was active for several years. “I met Rudiger in Wuppertal, that was a new jazz center by itself thanks to Peter Brötzmann and Peter Kowald,” wrote Gorter. “Sometimes I stayed at the studio that he shared with guitar wizard Hans Reichel. When Irene and Rudiger started playing together, they asked me to join and we played many places in the early ‘70s, with Heinrich Hock, Louis Moholo, or Alan Bateman on drums.” That band made only one full album, 1974’s Goose Pannée (FMP) but did have a track on the For Example - Workshop Freie Musik 1969 - 1978, the FMP boxed set.

1974-75 was an important period for two other reasons. Besides the aforementioned collaborations as well as work with the Boy Edgar Big Band and the small groups of Maurice Horsthuis and Toon van Vliet, Gorter was one of the musicians who helped establish Amsterdam’s Bimhuis, ultimately one of Europe’s premier venues for avant garde music, performing on its October 1st, 1974 opening night with the Burton Greene Quartet. Then in March 1975, Breuker asked Gorter to be a member of his Kollektief. Gorter described the group’s music as such: “Willem’s music had a lot of freedom. There were often tightly arranged written sections that would suddenly end and then the fun was to play on as if the arrangement continued – there was usually no such thing as chord changes – or to let the thing fall off a cliff ... Anyway, the music always felt fresh to play, even after many concerts, and there was a great mix of individual input and group discipline and cooperation. The Kollektief’s music linked the recognizable to the unexpected, often in 90-degree turns. It was surprising but accessible. For us musicians there was a wide spectrum of activities, from theater plays to movie music to interpretations of classical music and a lot of traveling to places where we found appreciative audiences, ranging from Australian school children to Chinese businessmen.”

The Kollektief would go on to make over three dozen albums, mostly released on Breuker’s BV Haast label, and perform all over the world, including during the Klap op de Vuurpijl (roughly, Top It All Off) Festival, taking place over five days at the end of each year from 1976-2005. Its book mixed Breuker and other band member pieces with tunes from various pages of the Great American Songbook and drawn from the classical canon, as well as other sources, presented in a highly theatrical manner best appreciated live and mixing in humor in refreshing contrast to the dour stage demeanor of many an improviser.

As busy as the Kollektief would keep him, Gorter still pursued other projects, some including fellow Kollektief members, including Breuker, and only existing on stages, such as groups under the leadership of Maarten van Norden, Sean Bergin, Boy Raaymakers, Pierre Courbois, Nedly Elstak, Jasper van ‘t Hof, Misha Mengelberg, and others. A representative sampling of those can be found in the archive of the Bimhuis (https://www.bimhuis.nl/archief); when he was in Amsterdam, this would be Gorter’s home near his home.

But there were also ones documented as albums: Maine, the 1975 collaboration of American trombonist Roswell Rudd with Dulfer, Gorter, and drummer Martin van Duynhoven, was made up of music by Sonny Rollins and Rudd (who had been coming to and working in the Netherlands since the mid ‘60s both with the New York Art Quartet and also locals like Loevendie). There were two 1977 dates by Cuypers, Zeeland Suite also including another bassist in South African expatriate Harry Miller; the 1979 Maarten Van Norden/Boy Raaymakers quartet date Chicken Song, completed by drummer Peter Nykyruj (of Mike Osborne fame); and a pair of 1980 albums spearheaded by the aforementioned trumpeter/composer Elstak (and released on his Coreco label; Gorter had loosely studied harmony with him in the ‘60s): To Build was led by Soesja Citroen’s name, who was one of five singers alongside Elstak, Breuker, Gorter, and Van Duynhoven for Sad Trumpets. The most significant, at least in terms of international exposure, came in July 1984, when Gorter, Mengelberg, and Bennink joined forces with two Americans, soprano saxophonist Steve Lacy and trombonist George Lewis, for the Soul Note release Change of Season (Music Of Herbie Nichols). Another important recording came 13 years later with Legendary: The 27th of May 1997, in a reunion with Hampel, who was fêting his seminal Heartplants SABA album from 1965 with original participants Courbois, Schlippenbach, and Schoof, Gorter standing in for his late friend Buschi Niebergall. One interesting takeaway from this is that it is often thought that after Breuker split with his fellow Instant Composers Pool founders Mengelberg and Bennink there were two distinct worlds in Dutch avant garde jazz; however, there were musicians like Gorter who operated in both spheres.

The new millennium found Gorter in several new projects: the mostly American blues/jazz band New Texas Swing from American saxophonist and then fellow Kollektief member Alex Coke with singer Tina Marsh and drummer John Betsch; the aptly named though horn-heavy Drummers Double Bill from Arend Niks and Verdurmen; 2000 recording The Compositions Of Eric Dolphy (BV Haast) with Coke, Breuker, Eric Vloeimans, Frank van Bommel, and John Engels; and Bo Van De Graaf’s I Compani; and the Rahsaan Roland Kirk “tribute” band Reeds & Deeds, also put together by Van De Graaf.

The Dolphy project had a personal resonance for Gorter, more specifically a much younger version of himself. In 1964, when he was 16, Gorter attended the Charles Mingus Sextet performance at Amsterdam’s Concertgebouw, a band with Dolphy, Johnny Coles, Clifford Jordan, Jaki Byard, and Dannie Richmond, which Gorter calls “the best ever ... Halfway through a trumpet solo by Johnny Coles, Eric left the stage while playing and walked into the hall. He ended up right next to my seat, way in the back. For a 16-year-old, that may have been a life-changing experience.” In 2011, Gorter was given the opportunity to celebrate Dolphy once more with a concert at the Bimhuis: “Eric Dolphy at The Five Spot Revisited,” with the legendary recording’s repertoire played by himself, Tom Arthurs, Rudi Mahall/Alex Coke (as his bass clarinet and saxophone/flute sides), Benoît Delbecq, and John Betsch.

Gorter joined the multimedia ensemble I Compani, founded by Van De Graaf in 1985, in 2010. As he wrote, “Bo van de Graaf just called it quits for I Compani, which I understand but regret. He led that band for 40 years through great adventures and I was happy to participate since 2010 or so. If anyone is comparable to Breuker in the amount of initiatives he took, it is him. Original pieces are blended with film music and live video, in various lineups from septet to 18-piece band. His music has the space, freedom and versatility of Breuker’s, but in a different way. Fun!”

When asked about the European scene in which he came up, Gorter replied, “At that time every European city had a very original and recognizable improvised music scene, or a few of them, like London with both the Spontaneous Music Ensemble and Brotherhood of Breath,” he wrote. “And they all had international contacts and were sharing with each other. So, the originality of these approaches, and the mutual respect, encouraged the exchange between countries and scenes and the musicians and their supporters took the initiative to made it happen.”

As for his own methodology towards, as shown in this piece, the variety of musical situations in which he has taken part, Gorter spoke both simply and profoundly: “From the beginning I played both free improvisation and tunes based on chord changes. Learning on stage was an option in the ‘60s, which sometimes led to embarrassment but more often to improvement. My approach is: first try to play what you hear, then figure out what others call it (= music theory), then apply that to play better what you hear and so on. Nowadays much education starts on the second step ...”

items.body:
This column is a loose gathering of recordings – two duos, two quartets – that might define a certain frontier, a degree of meaning in improvised interactivity spreading over 12 years. At times, the combination of close listening and simultaneous writing (the only way I can find to describe this music) results in verbal collisions that may be elusive in meaning, but they may also legitimately represent some of the transformative complexity and overlapping visions arising in these works of essentially collective invention. Though one of these recordings is more than a decade old, they may represent a kind of perpetual edge.

Certain musics can pass through walls of custom, identity, and meaning, assuming unknown shapes, escaping any strict verbal denotation, meaning becoming at once plastic and ineffable. Such music cannot be analyzed or described successfully, such failed exercises, however, perhaps contributing to both its mystery and its beauty, music that might suggest a hymn from an unknown culture, possibly disappeared, to an unknown deity, possibly deceased. In collectively improvised music, the role of the listener is paramount: assembling, collecting, composing ... At the same time, however, no interpretation is more privileged than another. These particular recordings are by musicians who can create dreams in sound. Some will imagine mills or factory floors, tuned to and amplifying unimaginable inventions of human industry. Empathy contributes a mutating, transformational soundscape. These are musics that create uncommon space.

Die Dritte Ebene (45 rpm LP, NiVuNiConnu, nvnc-lp062) by Emilio Gordoa and the late Sven-Åke Johansson might initially seem exotic. Ultimately, it’s not. It’s work of perfect transparency, that is, a view of whatever one hears as the other side of anywhere. The cover offers two titles, DIE DRITTE EBEN or EL TERCER NIVEL, “the third level,” in German or Spanish, with each phrase written with the “E”s written as reversed 3s. The phrase arises in Gordoa’s brief description appended to the Bandcamp page: “We were discussing how our music moves as if in parallel lines, and how after a while something third will emerge from it, almost like a ghost. It is something I find almost mystical: how this third level manifested itself in our playing without us thinking about it.”

Reminiscent of Johansson’s previous NiVuNiConnu release, Tea Time, with Nicholas Bussmann and Yan Jun, the music hints at Erik Satie’s Furniture Music, somehow constituting a radical background music that enhances consciousness, the special resonance of repeated materials creating a trance-like, near-ecstatic state, a reflective consciousness that rises between the parts created by Johansson and Gordoa, illuminating as well as hypnotic. Die Dritte Ebene, from August 26, 2023, points to an ineffable quality – a kind of trance, a kind of lift, a spectral point of attention that is produced in a listener’s collaboration with the close echoes, tight resonance and metallic rattle of Johansson’s snare, the reeds of his accordion, and the glassy ring of Gordoa’s vibraphone, glowing like light in sonic form. The shared insistence and simultaneity of Johansson and Gordoa’s work consistently expands what is essentially a minimalist musical environment, concluding with a strange abstraction of accordion and vibraphone that might suggest a kind of musical haunting.

Nate Wooley and Seymour Wright recorded About Trumpet and Saxophone in 2012, appearing on the Fataka label in 2013. While that release was unquestionably radical, its forthcoming successor, recorded in 2025, About Saxophone and Trumpet (Relative Pitch) takes a very different initial tack, opening with a deconstruction of the romantic ballad “The Midnight Sun,” composed by Lionel Hampton and Sonny Burke in 1947, recorded initially as an instrumental, with sufficient melodic grace to have lyrics later added by Johnny Mercer, spurring recordings by June Christy, Ella Fitzgerald, and Carmen McRae. Here the melody is clearly audible through a series of gasps, honks, and shattered, incomplete phrases, a nod to tradition that rapidly expands, becoming increasingly inclusive.

There follows “Experiment Four,” an extended dialogue which includes some of the strangest sounds ever emitted by saxophone and trumpet, often coming from very different positions in the sound spectrum. The fourth track, “Untitled,” is genuinely conversational, though the conversation is conducted in assorted bleats and blasts. Each musician is repeatedly triggered by the other’s material, whether pinching their sound inward, or adapting a radical extroversion. Music here will stand in for complex human relationships and perceptions, a sound store evolving to mark the impact of events in one’s daily life, worlds for which artists have long been refining their techniques and perceptions. As our descriptive apparatus daily fails before global events, our key artists stretch the elements. In that sense, call it modern syntactical practice or a soundtrack to Guernica, but the expressive range in which Wooley and Wright here operate seems perfectly in keeping with the daily news. Meanwhile, the inner tunings and sustained tones, even their matching fast vibratos suggest the development and synergy of an expressionist language. Sudden shifts will swiftly resemble elegant balladry of yore, echoes of that “Midnight Sun.”

While the Wooley/Wright duet recalls Fataka, Trevor Brent’s remarkable label – “‘dedicated to releasing recordings of small group and solo improvisations with a particular interest in situations where a common musical language has not yet fully emerged” – has become active again, releasing Parallels & Diagonals by a quartet from the label’s earlier period, 14th July 2014 at Cafe Oto, in which Wooley and Wright appear in a quartet with two percussionists active since the dawn of English free improvisation, Paul Lytton and Eddie Prévost. Contrary to Brent’s explanation of the label (and a genuine generational difference: the percussionists had discographies before the wind players were born), the four musicians seem so closely attuned – each a genuine spontaneous composer – that they sound like they might have had a long history together. Parallels and Diagonals is 12-year-old music, but it sounds like it might be recorded next year.

The opening track, the extended Parallel A, sounds like a machine shop that has discovered free improvisation, shifting dramatically after a passage of silence shortly after the 15-minute mark. The sounds suggest a light roll on a kettle drum, a brush on a cymbal, the sound of air pushed delicately through a trumpet. This notion of interiority marks the collective passage of these musicians, finding a terrain at once both barely imagined and yet a defining part of the human condition. In Diagonal A, fundamental gestures, like air squeezed through a metal tube, take on their own significance, behaving like Buddhist mudras, invoking fundamental gestures and symptoms of human life, murmurs, signs, abrasions. Diagonal B’s rapid actions and continuous overlapping suggest activity so closely attended by the musicians that it might follow a score in which the pauses might be carefully accounted, floating among a delicately bowed cymbal, other sounds that cannot be identified, and some that shimmer around audibility.

foam and mesh (Fundacja Słuchaj Records) by the B:A:N:S BAND is the work of pianist Sophie Agnel, saxophonist John Butcher, bassist Pascal Niggenkemper, and percussionist Ståle Liavik Solberg, recorded at the 2024 ArtAct Festival in St. Johann, Austria. While it’s the only grouping here with a conventional instrumental grouping, the orientation of the musicians will ensure that there is nothing resembling convention in the ways that the instruments are utilized.

foam and mesh I is clearly the main event, a 35-minute dialogue in which four of the most skilled spontaneous composers put together a dense weave of sonic events, with nothing predictable, yet everything interlocking. Tension curves are developed with astonishing power, each member of the quartet seemingly pursuing a unique and independent path, yet everything contributing to an astonishing rhythmic taffy-pull in which every part contribute to a compound and original overall momentum. This complex relationship will sustain through numerous group movements, whether slow balladic ruminations with isolated knocks and flurries or a sudden tense wedding of trembling oscillations, all four musicians regularly finding distinct timbres. The relatively brief foam and mesh II initially foregrounds Agnel’s piano, her focus initially on brief, isolated, tight-knit clusters with abstract flurries from Niggenkemper’s bass and the randomizing knitwork of Liavik Solberg. When Butcher initially enters on soprano saxophone, the random patterns generally coalesce into a continuous stream of different rhythms and complementary densities before the work’s ultimately gradual disappearance.
items._cn_summary: 本文评论四张集体即兴录音作品，涵盖两组二重奏与两组四重奏，横跨十二年，展现即兴互动中的前沿探索。作者强调这种音乐无法用语言严格描述，介于可塑与不可言说之间，听众的参与与组装至关重要。评论聚焦于Emilio Gordoa与已故Sven-Åke Johansson的二重奏专辑《Die Dritte Ebene》，二人通过近距离聆听与同步写作创造出第三层次的幽灵般涌现，音乐呈现出萨蒂家具音乐式的背景质感，又带有近乎出神的催眠状态，在重复材料的特殊共鸣中生成反思意识。这种透明的声音既奇异又神秘，让听者得以窥见音乐背后那个超越任何一方的第三维度。

items.body:
Gerry Hemingway leads a band of globe-trotters: German multi-reedist Frank Gratkowski whose recorded in the US often; pianist Izumi Kimura based in Ireland; Swiss bassist Christian Weber who’s recorded on three continents, crossing paths along the way with Yanks Oliver Lake, Ellery Eskelin, Nate Wooley, and Russ Johnson; Gerry himself, based in Lucerne since 2009.

In many ways Hemingway’s contemporary music mines his time in Anthony Braxton’s wondrous 1985-1993 quartet. The leaping staccato melody with asymmetrical phrases near the top of the 36-minute “Bau 4 Assembly” is one marker; another, the way that loose suite and the 23-minute “Slivers” use long improvised sections to tie together occasional scored episodes – not that Braxton was alone in that. And Braxton’s quartet prompted Hemingway’s duo with bandmate Marilyn Crispell, prefiguring his duo with Kimura in recent years.

On the CD, a six-minute Hemingway-Kimura improvisation is sandwiched between the long pieces, but I tend to cue up that “Third Story Variation” first, for its unbeatable interplay. The pianist and drummer catch and ride the same pulse, leaving plenty of air but also knowing how to fill various spaces along the way. Their timbral senses are fully compatible: her under-the-hood preparations tilt her sound drumward. They’ll set up a slow groove together, then she’ll use her other hand to play against it. It’s all very attentive and effective.

The longer pieces credited to Hemingway unfold like narratives, with discreet episodes, varied pacing, subgroup subplots, ways to build and dispel tension. “Slivers” is for trio, minus piano, Gratkowski leading off on squawky bass clarinet, tracked by Weber’s bass; the time feel is notably looser than the duo’s. A few minutes in, bass clarinet exits, and Frank’s re-entrance on disembodied wispy alto is placed just right: an instant orchestrator’s decision. Later there’s a section for low bass clarinet and arco bass in frictive unison under free drum rustle – suggesting Braxton’s love of the sub-basement, and the flexible trio dynamic of Gerry’s early/longtime vehicle BassDrumBone. But “Slivers” does slack off a bit between the scored tentpoles. There are times you wish the drummer would apply a firmer hand in a what-would-Billy-Higgins-do kind of way. One of Gerry’s signatures at the traps is a free-swinging–arms sense of relaxation, hitting the skins as if on the rebound, with some hits maybe dropped or delayed in transit. In the closing minutes, and on the closing theme, he can come off like someone who thinks he’s swinging harder than he is.

All four assemble for “Bau 4 Assembly” which makes up the bulk of the program. The venue Bau 4 in Altbüron, Switzerland was founded by folks in the timber business, and is located in their commercial compound. In tribute, Gerry and company play or use as beaters wood scraps retrieved from the workshop, notably heard around 10 minutes in, on a fast irregular clacky and texturally light colloquy which develops into something like pointillism with a groove (no small achievement) before flute and pedal-down piano soften things up. But not for long; in very short order, a scrapwood and piano gamelan. Midway, there’s a long-tone chapter with clarinet, and Gerry singing wavery lines into his cymbals or (says here) through metal objects, an odd effect he just about pulls off. (There’s a little Robert Wyatt in his vocal wah-wahs.) The composer and the quartet cover much ground. Elsewhere, a slow line’s melodic contours are subtly mirrored by the drums.

We won’t catalog every change-up or chapter, but near the end there’s a free-jazz blowout whose presence feels like checking a box – which is not to overlook Frank’s rapid multiphonic growls. (He’s got a great command of altissimo and pressurized reed textures.) Then they break into a loose brisk tempo, to frame that free-jazz energy. It arrives just where a non-drummer’s band would place a climactic the drum solo. Then a feint toward the Braxtonian head from half an hour earlier. A few staccato hits end things without a big fuss.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由鼓手Gerry Hemingway领衔，集合德国多管乐演奏家Frank Gratkowski、爱尔兰钢琴家Izumi Kimura与瑞士贝斯手Christian Weber四位跨地域音乐人。作品深受Hemingway在Anthony Braxton四重奏时期的影响，采用预构段落与长篇即兴交织的结构方式。36分钟的《Bau 4 Assembly》以不对称乐句展开叙事，二十三分钟的《Slivers》为钢琴缺席的三重奏编制，低音单簧管与贝斯的摩擦性齐奏呼应Braxton对极低音域的偏爱。Hemingway与Kimura的六分钟二重奏展现高度默契的互动，钢琴家的延伸技法使音色向鼓体靠拢。专辑录制于瑞士木材厂改造的演出空间Bau 4，乐手使用废弃木料作为打击素材，赋予作品独特的物质质感与场地回响。整体呈现出学院派自由爵士的结构思维与即兴能量之间的平衡探索。

items.body: Music For Drifting is the debut LP from Aase Frejadóttir. Releasing on Editions Verde, and using synthesizers, field recordings, strings, and voice, Frejadóttir’s music isn’t afraid to switch things up. Straight off the bat, her music feels incredibly expansive while also remaining intimate and warm. There’s no doubt that the warmth is due to the synth, and it radiates from it, but its soft swells and the emergence of a new melody also helps to provide a benevolent atmosphere of awe and wonder that fits in with the warmer sound. Whether walking her dog, Pulsar, or drifting through the forests on the outskirts of Stockholm, Aase’s music appears to be a free spirit, in search of something more: extracting deeper meanings from the music, which is a glowing stream of distant light. A lover of Astronomy from an early age, Aase’s music is interwoven with the black fabric of space, containing material from an infinite beyond, and she builds her spacious music upon its bedrock – the glowing light of dead stars and something of the cosmic is audible in her music. Strings burst forth and a radiant harmony bursts onto the scene with the royal elegance, grace, and supreme force of a bejewelled supernova. Her music is constantly shifting, turning, its refractions and reflections rebounding and moving from note-to-note. Everything is tied to the Universe and the greater unknown, but although wide open arms and spatial possibilities are present on Music For Drifting, Aase never loses touch with what she and seven billion others call home, as heard in the more familiar, meteorological music of rain. That deluge of rain opens up ‘Dimma Promenad’, bringing us back to the soil and the earth, before transitioning into standout piece ‘Solemn Oath’ – twenty minutes of sweeping, orchestrated movements and patient drones. Cascading melodies glint and gently oscillate, and although the piece centres on a cluster of notes, it manages to evoke a ton of space and a reverential air fitting for a sacred oath. The notes are as pure and blessed as Holy Water. Following on is ‘Aerial’, which, with its additional layering, immediately counter-balances the previous piece. It favours depth over a skeletal fragility, and plump notes over a slimmer variant. Companionship and friendship over a solitary, long-forgotten corner of space, like the Earth’s positioning in the Milky Way. The mood is one of reflection and contemplation, not looking to figure things out with scientific equations or facts about the Universe, but rather revelling in its being. One can believe in the theory of an animated Universe when listening to her music. It’s enjoying existence for what it is: glorious, painful, tragic, thrilling. EV008: Music for Drifting by Aase Frejadóttir www.editionsverde.bandcamp.com
items._genre: ambient / drone / contemporary classical / field recording
items._cn_summary: Aase Frejadóttir首张专辑以合成器、田野录音、弦乐与人声为素材，呈现出宏大而温暖的声音景观。作品围绕宇宙、星空与自然意象展开，旋律在缓慢的涌动中不断展开，类似漂浮于太空或雨中的沉思状态。二十分钟的'Solemn Oath'是核心曲目，以管弦乐式铺陈与持续音为核心，旋律在音符群中闪烁振荡，营造出神圣肃穆的氛围。'Aerial'则转向纵深感，以更厚实的层次平衡前曲的空灵。整张专辑在宇宙主题与地球感之间游走，雨声采样与弦乐爆发交替出现，既保持亲密的温度，又延展出无垠的空间感。Editions Verde这一小厂牌发行的作品展现了鲜明的个人美学，适合沉浸式聆听。
