items.body: For this release on Canadian label caduc, Ryoko Akama, Cristián Alvear, Cyril Bondi, and d’incise perform Taku Sugimoto’s “mada”. The first section features pin-pricks of guitar punctuating controlled feedback, harmonium, and bowed metals, each instrument following its own line of single tones, but each modifying perceptions of the pitch, speed, and duration of all the others. Everything moves slowly, quietly. You have to slow down to catch these perceptions — slow down your thoughts, your heart rate, your expectations. Sometimes the tones may disappear completely, due to their own low volume, the masking of other noises in the environs, or your own mind racing ahead and losing the thread. You get the impression that’s ok though. The second section is five minutes of silence, while the third and final one picks up where the first left off, introducing piano and percussion in the place of harmonium and bowed metals. The slowly changing combinations of tones and timbres could be compared to a kind of topology: contours rising and falling in pitch and volume, creating undulating slopes, sharp peaks, and flat valleys of silence. To say that the sounds occur at random is like saying a landscape rises and falls at random. It may well appear that way to you given that you didn’t see the millennia of water and wind erosion that gave rise to the topology now before you; yet some sense of logic is still dimly intuitable, a logic that any geologist would be able to explain. ‘Mada’ means ‘still’ in Sugimoto’s native Japanese, and the stillness of the piece contributes to the landscape-like nature of each section. The performance recorded by Akama, Alvear, Bondi, and d’incise is entrancing, with well-chosen sounds combined with precise control and subtlety. Their deep understanding of the music and of each other’s playing makes what could have been a dull, shapeless exercise into an absorbing panorama of sound. In today’s compulsively frenetic and cacophonous world, stillness is as rebellious and counter-cultural as it is rare; the still contours of music such as “mada” reveal the flatness of everything else.     Taku Sugimoto Ryoko Akama Cristián Alvear Cyril Bondi d’incise caduc
items._genre: experimental / avant-garde / reductionism / contemporary classical / improvisation
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑呈现了极度缓慢而克制的聆听体验。演奏者们以单音吉他反馈、簧风琴、弓拉金属、钢琴与打击乐器展开各自独立的线条，声音之间相互改变彼此的音高、速度与时值感知。整部作品被分为三个部分：首段是稀疏的音色交织，中段为五分钟的完全静默，末段接续首段的逻辑引入新乐器组合。乐评将这种缓慢变化的音色组合比作地形学——高低起伏的轮廓、尖锐的峰值与平坦的沉默山谷，暗示着某种深层但难以言说的逻辑。标题「mada」在日语中意为「静止」，与当下喧嚣嘈杂的世界形成对照。演出展现出对声音的精准控制力与彼此间的深层默契，将本可能枯燥无形的练习转化为引人沉浸的声景全景。

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.
items.label: Cool Waters
items._genre: folktronica / world fusion / experimental electronic / African traditional
items._cn_summary: 这张作品由驻肯尼亚的德国打击乐手与肯尼亚传统歌手及搭档共同完成，是内罗毕新厂牌的首发作品。核心亮点在于八十三岁传统肯尼亚dodo歌唱与Buchla合成器、手打打击乐及电子节奏的深度交织。编曲思路是让电子层逐层渗透进声部之中，从最初的简约重复节奏逐渐叠入4/4拍击、低音振荡与木琴音色，最终使合成多节奏与原始人声形成浑然一体的有机整体。乐评特别强调，这种合作模式体现了不同文化之间的真正对话——传统既未被现代手段碾压，电子技术也未喧宾夺主，而是让根源音乐获得前沿质感、让创新成果呈现古老的纵深。在文化传承层面，这张专辑也意味着一位耄耋歌手首次进入全球听众视野。整体来看，这是一次融合深度与开放性的跨文化实验成果。

items.album: Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari
items.artist: Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy
items.excerpt:
Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release,
Under an Endless Sky
.
In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari,

Francesco Paolo Paladi
items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. The title track from the 2023 U.S. of Alchemy recording Under an Endless Sky by Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy Further reading Cris Derksen - The Visit (Review) Tiny Sun - Vanishment (Review) Maria Ka - Di Mashin (Review) Further listening You will find a number of Dorothy Moskowitz's works on Race The Sky , most recently on Podgrammes #022 and #019.
items.label: Songs of Compassion
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由Dorothy Moskowitz与意大利合作者Francesco Paolo Paladino及Luca Chino Ferrari共同呈现。十一声部以钢琴为核心，辅以弦乐、木管与合成器音效织体，采用非线性和无调式化手法，挑战听众对西方和声运动的固有认知。Melody如意识流般起伏，不遵循传统调性进展，而是强调每个词的独立价值。歌词兼具政治性与哲思，从对威权主义的反思到对死亡与人类位置的冥想，延续六十年代抗议歌曲传统。Moskowitz的嗓音沧桑而权威，钢琴则像希腊悲剧中的合唱队般评述整体叙事。整体作品在政治分裂的时代回溯实验根源，将社会批判与音乐实验紧密交织。

items.body: Review by arcane-beautiful — Terrifying Angels by Pure Reason Revolution sees the band making their darkest and heaviest album to date, but still keeping specific musical quirks that the band are known for. Taking their new prog sound into elements that include dark ambient, nu metal, psychedelic, symphonic and alternative rock, it proves that Jon Courtney's project still has heavy weight and impression. The trade off of vocals between Courtney & Annicke Shireen are mixed perfectly, with great depth and tone, while musically the band explore all aspects of their sound, making this a true stand out in their discography. While the longer tracks are the true attention grabbers, the shorter songs do keep to their more classic sound with heavier elements. I'd give this a low to mid 8 out of 10. The track I'd recommend is Terrifying Angels.
items._genre: crossover prog / dark ambient / nu metal / psychedelic / alternative rock
items._cn_summary: Pure Reason Revolution 在这张专辑中展现了前所未有的黑暗与厚重质感，将新派前卫摇滚的骨架与暗潮氛围、新金属的重量感、迷幻元素及交响化编曲相融合。男女双主唱交替演绎构成核心张力，声线在阴郁与爆发之间切换，音色层次具有相当深度。乐队并未放弃自身的标志性怪癖，而是将这些特质推向了更极端的方向。长篇曲目承担了主要的艺术野心，短小作品则保留了乐队更经典的段落结构并叠加更沉重的器乐处理。整体制作在保持前卫摇滚可听性的同时，大幅拓展了声音光谱的阴暗区域，对于偏好实验与暗潮交叉地带的听众而言是一次有意义的探索。

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — One of the many one and done acts that emerged in Germany's fertile Krautrock scene actually lastedfrom 1973 when it formed in Bottrop until the band folded in 1980. While only releasing one album,1975's BROKEN DOOR, the band went through many lineup changes with only one version of the bandmanaging to record and release something but even though a single album was recorded and set tovinyl, it was produced in such low numbers that it was virtually forgotten shortly after its releasealthough the band did frequent the live circuits for its entire run. Luckily BROKEN DOOR was rescuedby the Garden of Delights label and has emerged as one of those unexpected gems that was almostcompletely lost to history.With a rather contradictory band name juxtaposed to a disheartening album title, PROSPER wassomewhat unique and whereas some German prog was not Krautrock and not all Krautrock wasprogressive, PROSPER found the nice in-between zone that allowed the headier atmospheric texturesand spaciness of the koschmische sounds exist in full space rock mode all the while offering anabundance of virtuosic instrumental moments mostly courtesy of guitarist Evert Brettschneider whowas concurrently active in the jazz fusion group Contract Trio. Not surprisingly some of thisjazziness seeped into PROSPER which works surprisingly well. Add some King Crimson grit to the mixand you're in for a real treat with this one.The album is primarily instrumental dishing out a multitude of space rock-tinged motifs laced withmoments of progressive rock heft and jazzy accouterments. The band was a five-piece but implementeda diverse array of guitar tones (both acoustic and electric) as well as a plethora of keys rangingfrom the Fender Rhodes and Mini-Moog to mellotrons and other electronic effects however the thumpingbass grooves clearly point to Amon Dull II's heady mix of kosmische kraftiness. The album featuredeight tracks which range from softer contemplative space rock to more jazz-fueled prog. The opening"Beginning" offers a nice rotisserie of all the styles on the menu and elegantly passes the batonfrom one genre shift to another. The band's dexterity in handling the instrumentation allows thealbum to take on a more epic feel as opposed to many Kraut acts that were simply going for theescapist approach.While the album is fairly uniform in its feel, the mid-album clunker "Your Country" sounds woefullyout of place with its country rock style that wouldn't have sounded out of place on an album fromThe Band and although competently performed somewhat derails the momentum of the album's continuityhowever the surrounding material is strong enough to allow the listener to merely shrug it off assome kind of unfortunate anomaly. Overall PROSPER's debut release is indeed a true gem that took thebest aspects of the varying Krautrock and prog styles of the era and seamlessly agglutinated it allinto a cohesive sound of its own right. This is indeed a band that should've released another albumor two before evaporating into the 1980s but like many bands of the day, we're actually lucky toeven have the opportunity to experience this one once rare and unknown band's sole artifact.
items._genre: krautrock / space rock / progressive rock / jazz fusion
items._cn_summary: PROSPER 1975年唯一专辑《Broken Door》融合了Krautrock的太空迷幻氛围与前卫摇滚的器乐张力，吉他手Evert Brettschneider同时活跃于爵士融合团体Contract Trio，爵士元素自然渗入。五人编制运用丰富的吉他音色与键盘层次，从Fender Rhodes、Minimoog到mellotron，配合贝斯线条营造出类似Amon Düül II的宇宙感力量。全器乐为主，八首曲目在太空摇滚与爵士前卫之间游走，开场曲巧妙串联各类风格转换。唯一的瑕疵是中段一首乡村摇滚风格曲目显得突兀，破坏了整体连贯性。专辑由Garden of Delights厂牌重新发掘，避免了几乎被历史遗忘的命运。整体将Krautrock与前卫摇滚的精华凝聚成独属自身的连贯声音，在统一氛围中展现器乐演奏的灵活性与史诗感。

items.body: John Coltrane - Olé (Atlantic, 1961) In the mid-1990s I had just graduated from undergrad with a degree in Journalism and absolutely no idea what to do next. I spent the following summer living in a shared house with five other people about my age, one of whom was a good friend and musical partner in our band called “ Joe Joe the Dog Face Boy. ” We were working, we were playing music, all in all, it was fine even if a bit of a confusing time in life. In the living room of the house, next to my room, was a shelf with a bunch of records on it. The records belonged to my friend, who had just been gifted them by his father. He had placed them on the shelf not knowing what to do with them - I am not sure that he even had a record player at this point, as it was the heyday of CDs afterall. I, however, did have a record player that had been accompanying me all through college and would be my only constant companion for the next twenty years or more, so the records, a rather eclectic mix of music from the 60s and 70s, would end up often on my stereo. This was how I encountered Ol é. Olé , John Coltrane’s last album for the Atlantic label, released in 1961, was recorded with his long-time associates MyCoy Tyner on piano and Elvin Jones on drums, which already likely brings certain harmonic and rhythmic sounds to mind. Joining them was trumpeter Freddie Hubbard, bassists Reggie Workman and Art Davis, and the great Eric Dolphy on flute and alto sax. It was the title track that caught my ear. Extending over the whole side A of the album, it’s a modal feast that builds on a vamp derived from a Spanish folk song. Here, it starts with a single churning bass line and Tyner’s pulsating chords balancing on Jones' driving swing. Soon, Coltrane joins on soprano sax with an approach reminiscent of his playing on ‘My Favorite Things.’ Then, Dolphy lends his flute to the mix, paving the way for Hubbard’s solo, from which the track really takes off. It was rhythmically dense music, but not overly dissonant or harsh; however, for ears that could listen to jazz but were more attuned to rock, it was the perfect hook - a little more advanced than what I was used to, but not too steep of a climb. The B-side’s, ‘Dahomey Dance’ and ‘Aisha’ were a bit more rooted in the ‘jazz’ I knew. I enjoyed them, but it was the A-side that pushed me as a listener. Critics have called Olé a transitional album. Aside from the label change, Coltrane was also headed towards more experimental realms. For me, Olé and that pile of records also came at a transitional time, and helped reveal new paths and possibilities. Thelonious Monk with John Coltrane (Jazzland, 1961) My plan was to next dig into something in that experimental realm. I had my sights on Offering: Live at Temple University, a live album recorded in 1966, shortly before Coltrane passed away, and released posthumously by Resonance Records in 2014. A funny thing happened, however, along the way. As I was pulling up the recording, I passed by Thelonious Monk with John Coltrane and stopped in my tracks. Also released in 1961 on the Jazzland label, this set of evergreen Monk tunes that had been recorded by Coltrane and Monk in '57 and '58 with changing rhythm sections. Two seconds of the opening ‘Ruby, My Dear’ and I knew I’d wanted to spend a little time awith this one again before moving on. As the story goes, Coltrane was addicted to heroin and had just been fired from Miles Davis’ group. He took this break, and cleaned himself up and started to play with Monk. A residency at the Five Spot in NYC in ‘57 is the stuff of legends and a concert recording of the two from 1957 was discovered and released in 2005 by Blue Note, lends credence to the stories. Entitled Thelonious Monk Quartet with John Coltrane at Carnegie Hall, it underscores the copacetic musical relationship found on the original release. Back to that recording: the tune that stopped me in my tracks, the slow moving ‘Ruby, My Dear’ begins with such a melancholic saxophone playing the yearning melody that it instantly romanticizes any space where it’s played. ‘Tinkle, Tinkle,’ with its playful and up-tempo melody gives Coltrane a chance to unfurl those ‘sheets of sound’ that he’s famous for. Similarly on ‘Nutty’, the sheets return in a generously flowing solo, studded at key points with with reminders of the melody. Drum and bass outlining the tune, Monk waiting to come back in with the melody, before abstracting it into Improvisational flurries. This album album is a high point in two musical catalogs that are festooned with them. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body: Strikkland are easy to misread if you mistake humour for distance. Henrik Johansson can deliver brutal lyrics while smiling, appear in a red feather boa, play with national flags or deliberately puncture the visual severity traditionally associated with EBM, but none of that suggests embarrassment about the genre. Quite the opposite. The joke works because the attachment underneath it is genuine. They are not standing outside EBM making fun of its conventions; they know those conventions intimately enough to interfere with them. I first saw the Gothenburg duo at E-Only in 2024 and again this year on the much larger Waldbühne at Nocturnal Culture Night. At NCN, something became particularly clear: humour had stopped feeling like something happening around the songs and had become part of Strikkland’s performance language itself. Hard electronic structures, Henrik’s forceful delivery and the physical directness of EBM remained intact, while gestures, costumes and irony continually destabilised the expectation that seriousness must look solemn. Their second album, “Hommage”, makes that tension especially interesting. It openly acknowledges the music that formed Henrik and Henric, while its production deliberately returns to hardware, physical studio equipment and recording practices associated with an earlier era. Yet Strikkland have little interest in turning EBM into heritage preservation. For them, tradition is useful precisely when it can still be disturbed. We spoke about growing into a band after fifty, refusing genre uniforms, why limitation can generate creativity, the ethics of AI, the strange authority of old symbols, and what happens when two people who take EBM very seriously refuse to behave as though seriousness requires a permanent scowl. Strikkland interview Karo: I first saw you at E-Only in 2024 and then again on the much larger Waldbühne at NCN this year. What struck me at NCN was how much more clearly humour had become part of the performance language itself. When did you realise that humour could be structural to Strikkland rather than merely something happening between songs? Henrik: We have always had humour as an important element of what Strikkland is all about. We started the band on impulse and as a fun thing to do. The lyrics are often conjured up at the same time as we are in the studio creating new songs. My texts often tend to drift towards dark stories about space, death, fantasy and the absurd. The humour you get from seeing the band live is something we have developed throughout all the time we have been on stage. We have fun, and that creates what we deliver. Henric: We realised early on that two old geezers would only look ridiculous if we tried to act tougher or darker than we actually are. Besides, there are plenty of bands already biting heads off chickens or dressing up in full combat gear on stage. It has all been done before, and it really didn’t seem like an option for us. Our appearance and the way we behave also evolved from criticism in Sweden after our first live shows in the early days: “Their music is half-decent, but they aren’t a real EBM band because they don’t look or behave like one.” We kind of turned that against the critics, embraced it even more and made it our thing. Karo: At NCN you told me that when you started the band, already approaching your fifties, you briefly considered becoming the “gothiest” band possible before deciding that pretending to be something you were not would be ridiculous. Did starting Strikkland later in life actually give you a kind of freedom younger bands sometimes lack, because you had less need to prove that you belonged? Henrik: Absolutely! Also, later in life you have so many more musical influences to choose from and try to implement into your own songs. Starting a band later in life also means you can afford to have a band and go places to play live without starving and sleeping in the car on the way there. We are doing something today that you thought impossible when you were young. Henric: Being close to 50 when you start a band certainly provides more freedom. Our ambition was never to release records or perform live, but when possibilities opened up, we jumped for it. Speaking for myself, I got a chance to do what I wanted to do in my teens but never got the chance to do. At 50, you aren’t as afraid of criticism or about what others might think as you are at 16 or 17. That helped a lot. Karo: EBM has accumulated a very strict visual and behavioural vocabulary: severity, discipline, confrontation, often a certain cultivated lack of humour. You clearly love the genre, but you also interfere with those conventions constantly. Which parts of EBM do you take completely seriously, and which parts do you think deserve to be laughed at? Henrik: We never laugh at EBM, but we think we can involve irony and humour in the genre and have a laugh at certain aspects of life. Humour and art are always found in the contrasts. I mostly write quite dark lyrics, but we present them with a lot of smiles, humour and dance. Henric: EBM has been a huge part of my life since the 1980s, so it is something I take very seriously. I do laugh at some of the rigidity coming from certain corners of the fanbase, though. Come on, loosen up and dance while you still can. Have fun. At least laugh a little. There are enough bitter middle-aged men in the world, and I don’t want to become one of them. Karo: That is also why “Hommage” interests me. It is explicitly a tribute to the music that formed you, but homage can easily become imitation. How do you honour an artistic language without treating it as something that should remain frozen in the period when you first discovered it? Henrik: The tribute to the EBM bands we grew up with is always there when we make music. In “Hommage”, it is in the basslines, the sounds, the technology and the artwork. I am a curious person, so I constantly look for new music and new bands to listen to. The EBM genre, and Strikkland, keep finding new ways without letting go of the legacy of the bands of the 80s. Henric: Apart from a handful of gems from bands like Kraftwerk, DAF, Nitzer Ebb, Front 242 and a few others which can’t be topped, EBM and electronic music have evolved a lot. In my playlists there are rarely any songs older than two or three years. You can still hear where it is coming from, but it has evolved. If we stick to what we grew up with, there would be stagnation and the genre would surely die out. But thanks to artists like SIIE, Emmon, Plastikstrom and many others, it is still interesting. So I would rather risk going outside the standard formula and at least try to contribute to keeping EBM alive, both musically and visually. Karo: You made “Hommage” deliberately with classic studio equipment, hardware synthesizers and drum machines, and you were very explicit about not using AI. Is that primarily an ethical position, an aesthetic one, or did you simply want the limitations of those tools to become part of the composition? Henric: AI has no place in art. Full stop. For both creative and ethical reasons. When it comes to using hardware versus working “in the box”, it is purely a workflow decision. The tactility of turning knobs and pushing buttons works better for me than using plugins. We are also privileged enough to get to work together with Hans Olsson at Svenska Grammofonstudion in Gothenburg, which is both a studio and a “synthesizer museum”. It would be stupid not to use all of those classic machines if you can. Our first album, “Bodypop”, was mixed there on an SSL 4000E console, so when we got the chance to mix “Hommage” at Hansa in Berlin on their SSL console, of course we took the plunge. And of course we did some additional recordings there as well. I mean, who could resist playing the very same Steinway grand piano that Martin Gore posed in his jocks next to? Karo: There is an interesting contradiction there: Strikkland describe themselves as expanding the borders of EBM, yet “Hommage” deliberately looks backwards in terms of production practice. Can technological limitation actually be more progressive than unlimited technological possibility? Henrik: Well, maybe in a way every EBM band today is expanding the borders of EBM? To stay in the genre, you have to remain within the frame agreed upon, regardless of what technology you use. But it gets more interesting if you drift away towards the border and sometimes cross it, bringing in other influences and expressions. That’s the way music has always evolved. Henric: For me, limitation sparks creativity. There is a certain number of available channels on a physical mixing console. On a computer, you can have hundreds. There are also limitations to hardware synthesizers and effects, and all of this forces me to be creative. As mentioned before, this is a workflow that suits me. With that said, most of our songs start out “in the box” because it is convenient. Karo: Henric writes the music and programming while Henrik handles vocals and lyrics. With such a clear division, where does the personality of a Strikkland song emerge? Does the music arrive with a character already inside it, or can the vocal idea fundamentally alter what Henric thought he had written? Henrik: Often we start with a bassline that Henric has created and then build it together from that point. I get inspiration for the lyrics and write them at the same time as Henric starts to develop the music. When both of us feel ready, we fuse it all together. This is a fast process, so we are very much in line with what kind of music we want to produce. Henric: Let’s put it this way: when Henrik enters the studio, I might have 20 loops that I have worked on for six months, with basslines, drums and maybe a melody ready. If Henrik says, “Great! But can we change this or that?”, that loop goes into the bin. But if he stops, shuts up and starts to write text immediately, I know it is a keeper. Then we combine that idea into a draft by making a rough arrangement, tweaking the text, tweaking the music and finally recording it. When we have enough tracks for an album, we take it to Hans and re-record everything. So, to answer your question, the music inspires the vocals and the vocals give direction to the final piece of music. Neither would be the same without the other. Karo: At NCN, Henrik changed clothes, exaggerated gestures and played with Swedish and German symbols and declarations of friendship. In a genre that has historically borrowed heavily from militarised imagery, does humour give you a way to use those symbols without allowing them to retain all of their old authority? Henrik: When I go to see a band live, I want to be entertained. When I am on stage, I want to entertain and have a good time! To joke around and interact with the audience and get a warm response elates me. I love the contrast of delivering hard-hitting music and brutal lyrics with a smile on my face and prancing around with a red feather boa. So yes, it is absolutely a way to deflate the power of symbols of power. Henric: Personally, I think it is important to reclaim symbols like national flags from fascists and extremists and use them in a positive way. We don’t hide behind humour and irony, but instead use them as tools for communication. Our message is clear. We don’t accept fascists, Nazis or totalitarian regimes, we support Ukraine’s fight for freedom and we advocate free speech. But maybe we have chosen a “lighter approach” to convey this than other bands, mainly because the darker image doesn’t suit us on a personal level. Karo: What I particularly liked was that none of this reduced the concert to parody because the musical foundation remained genuinely hard. Do you consciously protect that balance, making sure the joke never becomes an excuse for musical weakness? Henrik: When we make our music, we never implement humour to start with. Okay, some lyrics are rather absurd and some sound effects we add for fun, but we want our music to be serious and taken seriously. It is mostly when we play live that we joke around. Henric: Some people have clearly written us off as a parody act. No question about that! But either they haven’t seen us perform live or they haven’t understood what we are doing. Irony is a tough nut to crack for some, and others lack humour. One thing is certain, though. We would never release or perform anything that we ourselves thought was weak, and we put a lot of work into our music. Karo: You worked with Hans Olsson at Svenska Grammofonstudion and Hansa Studios on “Hommage”. Did working in spaces carrying so much recording history make you more conscious of tradition, or was the important thing precisely to forget the mythology once you were actually inside the studio? Henric: It took a while for it to sink in once we were at Hansa. We were actually sitting at the same mixing console that was used to make some of the greatest albums of my youth?! Insane! But once that feeling disappeared, it was just another day in the studio and we did our thing together with Hans. Henrik: Hans Olsson suggested mixing the album at Hansa, and I honestly was totally unaware of the history of this studio. Henric was jumping up and down with excitement. We were there for three days and it finally dawned on me how cool it was! There we could use the same machines and instruments that our heroes used. Karo: The larger stage at NCN seemed to suit you surprisingly well. Some electronic acts compensate for space by simply making every gesture bigger; with Strikkland, the additional room seemed to expose more of the interaction between you. Has playing larger stages changed the way you understand what the visual side of the band can do? Henric: We are not that used to playing larger stages. Apart from Subkultfestivalen in Sweden and WGT, most of our shows prior to NCN have been in front of a maximum of 200 to 300 people. I think there is a lot of room for visual improvement when playing the larger stages. We are just two guys and a couple of machines, so in order to put on even better shows we probably need some additional features on stage to make an impact. But we also don’t want to hide behind video walls, smoke and lasers. Guess it’s time to put on our thinking caps and find a Strikkland solution to the problem. But yeah, visuals are important to us, from album covers to how we appear on stage. Henrik: What Henric said. Karo: “Hommage” looked deliberately towards the music that made you. Looking ahead, what would be the opposite gesture? Is there something in the EBM tradition, perhaps even something you personally love, that Strikkland now need to leave behind in order to find out what the band can become next? Henrik: I can’t think of a thing in the EBM tradition that we want to leave behind. When we create new songs, all kinds of new influences colour the final result. Last time we met, the song rotated towards techno music, so who knows? I always get new ideas every time I listen to metal music. There you find my inspiration and trigger to do new stuff for Strikkland. But with that said, there will never be a guitar on stage with us. Body music forever! Henric: I don’t know, to be honest. There are most certainly no holy cows as far as Strikkland is concerned. What we would love to happen is to do even more shows in mainland Europe, and if that means we will have to tweak things one way or another, so be it. If it turns out we have to bite heads off chickens or perform in Pickelhauben in order to get booked, it might be worth a shot! I mean, a lot of people do judge books by the cover, and it would be sad to miss out because of that. We will see what happens and what we come up with. About Strikkland Strikkland are an electronic body music duo from Gothenburg, Sweden, consisting of Henric Ceder, responsible for music and programming, and Henrik Johansson, responsible for vocals and lyrics. Their first documented release, “Predatorial Right”, appeared on 27 March 2020. Their debut full-length album, “Bodypop”, followed on 2 December 2022. The ten-track record was mixed and mastered by Hans Olsson at Svenska Grammofonstudion in Gothenburg, using an analogue SSL 4000E console; Strikkland explicitly connected that production choice to their admiration for classic EBM. Their second full-length, “Hommage”, was released on 28 March 2025. The nine-track album was produced by Hans Olsson, with recording, mixing and mastering work carried out at Svenska Grammofonstudion in Gothenburg and Hansa Studios in Berlin. The band describe the album as a tribute both to the artists who inspired them and to older recording practices. They state that no AI was used in its production, relying instead primarily on classic studio equipment, hardware synthesizers and drum machines.

items.body: Delerium released the single “Into The Light”, featuring Diamanda Galás, on 23 September 2026 through Metropolis Records. It is the first single from Delerium’s new album “Exaudire”, set for release on 22 January 2027. Into The Light (with Diamanda Galás) by Delerium “Into The Light” incorporates portions of “Deliver Me From Mine Enemies”, written and performed by Diamanda Galás and included on her 1986 album “The Divine Punishment”, the American avant-garde singer’s Mute Records release that opened her “Masque of the Red Death” trilogy. The Delerium track sets that material inside the group’s own production, credited to founding members Bill Leeb and Rhys Fulber. “Exaudire” follows Delerium’s 2023 album “Signs” and carries twelve tracks, continuing the group’s format of pairing largely downtempo, atmospheric songwriting with a rotating cast of guest vocalists: Higher Power (with Mimi Page) Into The Light (with Diamanda Galás) Dream Palace (with Magic Wands) Buried Light (with Mimi Page) Apocalypse (with Inna Walters) Stolen (with Phildel) Into The Unknown (with Jaël) Multiplying Zero (with Inna Walters) Chasing The Wind (with Mimi Page) Exaudire Had To Go (with Jaël) Litany (with Mimi Page) About Delerium Delerium was founded in Vancouver, Canada, in 1987 by Bill Leeb and Rhys Fulber, both already active as members of the electro-industrial group Front Line Assembly. Where Front Line Assembly carried the pair’s aggressive, rhythm-driven material, Delerium became the outlet for their dark ambient and instrumental compositions, released through Dossier and Third Mind before the project moved to Nettwerk for its commercial breakthrough. From the mid-1990s onward, starting around “Semantic Spaces” (1994), Delerium began inviting guest vocalists to front largely downtempo songs on each album, a format the group has kept since. That approach produced its best-known track, “Silence”, featuring Sarah McLachlan, which reached number three in the UK singles chart following a series of 2000 remixes and won two Juno Awards for Best Dance Recording. Delerium music has since appeared in films including “Brokedown Palace” and “Lara Croft: Tomb Raider”, and “Silence” featured more recently in the BBC drama “Industry”. With Front Line Assembly already on the Metropolis Records roster, Delerium signed to the label for the albums “Mythologie” (2016) and “Signs” (2023). “Into The Light”, featuring Diamanda Galás, is the first taste of the follow-up, “Exaudire”, due on Metropolis Records on 22 January 2027.
items._genre: dark ambient / industrial / experimental electronic / downtempo

items.body: I’ll see you in the vacant light Somewhere in-between In a room that my body makes For you and me Some songs announce themselves with a manifesto. Violet Silhouette’s This Is Something seems perfectly happy admitting that nobody involved has quite figured out what the hell is happening yet. A chant catches against a taut backbeat, bass and drums immediately putting bodies in motion while the synthesizers maintain a cooler distance. There is some early Human League in that contrast between machine discipline and romantic uncertainty, while the repetitive rhythmic pull recalls LCD Soundsystem at their most economical. Violet Silhouette leave plenty of room around the beat, allowing repetition to become its own persuasive force. Five minutes later you may still have questions, although sitting down probably will not be among them. This Is Something catches the instant before certainty settles in: two people meeting somewhere between confession and possibility, with a dance beat underneath them and enough unanswered questions to keep things interesting. The song began with rhythm. According to the band, the drums and beat drove its development while melodies were tested until the track revealed its peculiar identity. Compared with much of their forthcoming album, VIVID(IS)DECAY, This Is Something leans further into dance music, though its lyrics occupy considerably less certain territory. With Lily Vile joining on bass, Violet Silhouette now operates as a trio, and that expanded physical presence suits material built so firmly around movement. The group formed in West Palm Beach in late 2019 and has since become geographically divided between South Florida and Austin. Distance has become part of their method rather than an impediment, with Dan and Zaii exchanging early ideas for VIVID(IS)DECAY beginning in 2024. Night provides the setting, but clarity remains elusive. Someone is trying to make sense of where they have been while simultaneously wondering whether knowing would accomplish anything useful. Desire can be detected before it can be understood; feelings exist before language catches up with them. There is hesitation throughout the verses, coupled with a growing willingness to let another person see what has previously remained private. Then Violet Silhouette introduce one of the song’s strongest images: two people meeting somewhere between recognizable states, inside a private room formed by the body itself. Suddenly This Is Something feels less like an evasive title and more like an admission. Whatever this connection is, somebody has finally acknowledged its existence. The accompanying video carries the uncertainty somewhere considerably stranger. Violet Silhouette initially perform inside gorgeous neo-film-noir compositions, bodies moving with the backbeat before strobes, abstract tableaux, and blurred recollections begin interrupting any comfortable sense of reality. “Visually, we drew from David Lynch’s Lost Highway,” says the band. “Our friend Roberto Badillo took our vision and ran with it — the result is sleek and visceral, like a gloved hand dragging desire across the table.” That glove fits. Watch the video for This Is Something below: Produced, mixed, and mastered entirely by Violet Silhouette, VIVID(IS)DECAY explores what the band calls Neuromanticism, their pursuit of truth and love through unstable identities, secret languages, and emotional dissolution. Listen to This Is Something below and order the single here. items._cn_summary: Violet Silhouette的《This Is Something》是一支以律动为核心的合成器驱动型曲目，贝斯与鼓机搭建出紧凑骨架，合成器保持冷感距离，呈现早期Human League式的机器纪律与浪漫犹疑之间的张力。重复节奏被刻意拉长，依赖循环本身的催眠效果推动身体运动，歌词则处于告白与可能性的模糊地带，描绘两人在身体所构成的私密空间中相遇的瞬间。歌曲以节奏先行，旋律随后逐步浮出，专辑《VIVID(IS)DECAY》中此曲偏向舞曲方向。伴随MV致敬David Lynch《Lost Highway》，以新黑色电影构图开场，随后被频闪、抽象画面与模糊记忆切割，现实感被持续打断。乐队2019年成立于西棕榈滩，目前以三人编制运作，跨越南佛罗里达与奥斯汀两地远程协作，地理距离反而成为创作方法的一部分。

items.body: Na skale Nad wodą Czaruje melodią For thousands of years, human beings have imagined voices calling to us from beyond the known world. The siren may be one of our oldest attempts to give desire a body. She waits at the boundary between land and sea, reason and longing, safety and surrender. Her song has power because the sailor brings something to it: loneliness, hope, curiosity, the wish to discover what lies beyond the horizon. Perhaps this is why the legend survives. The danger has never been merely the siren. It is our extraordinary capacity to hear, in the vast and indifferent world, precisely what we most wish were calling our name. Dawid Walkusz’s Syrena begins with the patience of something seen from a great distance: a bass line moving heavily beneath the surface, drums keeping a measured pace, and guitars and synths spreading a pale haze around Julia Frycz’s voice. The arrangement, channeling Current Joys, Cocteau Twins, Motorama, and Slowdive, belongs loosely to post-punk, coldwave, dreampop, and hypnagogic pop; though its strongest quality is less categorical than physical. The song seems to advance through water, every beat slightly burdened, every melodic phrase suspended between sleep and recognition. Frycz, a visual artist and vocalist with Emrere, gives Syrena its strange center of gravity. Her singing carries the calm authority of a figure who already knows how the story ends. Walkusz had written the instrumental and recorded early vocal parts before Frycz joined him, yet the collaboration feels unusually unified, as though both musicians had been picturing the same coastline without realizing it. Their subject is the siren, familiar from folklore as an emblem of beauty sharpened into danger, and the Polish lyrics render her with almost childlike clarity: she sits upon a rock above the water, her eyes glint, she appears angelic, and beneath the surface waits a tail. This simplicity gives the song room to become stranger. Sailors are drawn toward her by longing and tenderness, losing their way before affection itself becomes fatal. Walkusz and Frycz avoid turning the myth into theatrical gothic excess. The menace comes from softness, from the slow reassurance of the voice and the bass line’s stubborn tread. Desire becomes a navigational error. Love becomes a current capable of carrying someone farther than intended. The accompanying video extends this idea along the seaside, where cairns, stones, and open water create a setting suspended somewhere between Romantic poetry and Pre-Raphaelite painting. Frycz appears among the rocks as the siren, recalling the doomed women of Waterhouse and the river-bound Ophelia of Shakespeare, while Maciej Cimaszkiewicz’s cinematography favors natural forms over elaborate staging. Walkusz, who handled the editing and post-production, worked closely with Frycz to preserve the same visual language that had developed around the song. The shoreline becomes a psychological border, a place where the familiar world thins out and the sailor’s attraction begins to resemble surrender. Watch Syrena below: Syrena is the first glimpse of Walkusz’s second solo album, Fantometyka, due in spring 2027, and it suggests a broader, more confident development from his debut, Monochrom. The earlier record established his attraction to austere rhythms and blurred textures; here, those elements have acquired a more sensual sense of space. The song moves slowly, almost ceremonially, and its danger lies in how comfortable that pace becomes. By the time the siren has finished singing, the sailor’s fate feels less like catastrophe than consent. Listen to Syrena below, and order the single here. items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评围绕波兰音乐人Dawid Walkusz与歌手Julia Frycz合作的单曲展开。评论以古老的塞壬神话为切入点，将歌曲置于声学空间的隐喻中：贝斯线沉重如水下暗流，鼓点保持冷静节拍，吉他与人声周围漂浮着朦胧的合成器光晕。Frycz的声音带来一种预知结局的平静权威感，与Walkusz原本的器乐框架融为一体。波兰语歌词以近乎孩童般的清澈笔触描绘水边岩石上的塞壬形象，危险并非来自哥特式戏剧化，而是来自人声与低音线的柔和慰藉。MV延续这一概念，海边石堆、岩石与开阔水面构成浪漫主义诗歌与前拉斐尔派绘画之间的视觉空间，Cimaszkiewicz的摄影偏好自然形态而非刻意摆拍，海岸线成为心理边界。整体评论将音乐、神话、视觉三者编织为对诱惑与迷失方向的沉思。

items.body: Oh, holding on to yon and bitter falter Endless yearning weaves its web Among the forest, sheltered by her alter To be free, to be free Society of the Silver Cross draws on Gothic music’s old appetite for grand architecture, spiritual unease, and whatever might lie beyond ordinary daylight. Joe Reineke and Karyn Gold-Reineke built Temple of the Trees in Seattle, in part to accommodate that vision, filling the place with instruments that make a person wonder whether somebody has opened an archaeological dig beneath the control room. Their ongoing Temple Hymns series turns that studio into a meeting ground. Each installment brings another musician into the room to write and record with the pair, allowing personality, instinct, and whatever strange chemistry develops over several concentrated days to determine the results. Volume One brought in T.J. Cowgill of King Dude. For Temple Hymns Volume Two, Blood and Sun founder Luke Tromiczak flew from New York to Seattle and spent a week working with Reineke and Gold-Reineke. Tromiczak has led Blood and Sun since 2011, developing one of neofolk’s most recognizable baritones along the way. Put that voice beside twelve-string acoustic guitar, harmonium, B3 organ, Shahi Baaja, obscure synthesizers, and great booming toms and suddenly the room starts feeling considerably older than Seattle. Blood and Sun founder Luke Tromiczak Unraveled moves at the pace of somebody following a mountain trail after sunset with complete confidence that something significant waits at the other end. Its language circles freedom, transformation, lunar power, broken mirrors, concealed paths, and the promise of reunion. The arrangement carries the stateliness of Leonard Cohen into territory closer to Rowland S. Howard, while those deep drums suggest Ennio Morricone scoring some outlaw procession whose participants have traded revolvers for incense. The repetition in the vocal becomes nearly chant-like, working against the twelve-string guitar and organ until the track takes on a devotional character. Indian musical influence sits naturally beside American folk forms, giving the song an unusual spiritual geography. You can hear bits of Nick Cave, Nero Kane, and the Gun Club somewhere along the road, though everything has been dragged far enough into the Silver Cross universe to lose its passport. Battled Hands feels earthier, wounded by experience yet stubbornly pointed toward recovery in a call and response ballad. Tromiczak sings about endurance with the authority of somebody who understands that survival rarely comes accompanied by trumpets. Fire, dawn, damaged hands, storms, mercy, and returning light become markers along a long recovery from suffering. The slow progression allows each image enough room to settle before the drums push forward again. There is something almost physical about the weight of Tromiczak’s voice against the instrumentation. Reineke and Gold-Reineke surround him with enough space for every low note to feel carved into the room, while the harmonium and organ carry the devotional aspect further without turning the song into meaningless ceremony. Together, these two pieces make Temple Hymns Volume Two into a record of musicians discovering exactly how much ground they share. Listen to Temple Hymns Volume Two and order the double single here. Temple Hymns Vol. 2 by Society of the Silver Cross & Blood and Sun Society of the Silver Cross and Blood and Sun will take that meeting across Europe next month, where these songs should sound perfectly comfortable inside clubs, cellars, old halls, and any room willing to surrender its ordinary dimensions for a few minutes. items.body: There was always something faintly threatening about DEVO, even when they were dressed like escaped laboratory technicians and making middle America wonder whether Akron had been contaminated by industrial runoff. By 1984’s Shout, however, their absurdism had become so synthetically swollen that Puppet Boy could almost pass for another piece of mutant pop comedy. DEVO also have a long history of unconventional covers, from the classic Stones track I Can’t Get No Satisfaction, to Jimi Hendrix’s R U Experienced? Bex Delgado, recording as The Phantom Eyes, turns the tables on the Spud Boys: she hears the threat lurking inside Mark Mothersbaugh’s words and gives it a set of fangs. This version of Puppet Boy takes DEVO’s original premise and drags it into the bedroom of an especially disreputable vampire. The synthesizers feel colder and more severe, the rhythm carries a steady club-floor compulsion, and Delgado sings with the cool authority of somebody who already knows which end of the leash belongs in her hand. Mothersbaugh’s lyrics suddenly acquire an uncomfortable erotic logic. Obedience, dependency, affection, and ownership begin rubbing against one another until nobody seems especially interested in establishing boundaries. That change suits The Phantom Eyes remarkably well. Delgado approaches post-punk and dark electronic music through horror, where desire frequently comes with unfortunate contractual obligations and love can involve surrendering both your better judgment and access to daylight. There is humor inside it, too. Any cover of “Puppet Boy” that treats the title with complete solemnity would miss part of DEVO’s genetic code. Delgado preserves the perversity while turning the joke several degrees darker. The accompanying video makes the implication explicit. Filmed by Tori Kellogg/GR4VES in a single evening, it pairs Delgado’s scarlet entity with Sett’s Puppet Boy, a willing captive whose submission appears to have become his natural state. Red satin, CRT distortion, VHS degradation, and physical closeness give the footage the grubby glamour of an 80s vampire cassette discovered behind the counter of a video store that probably should have been investigated by local authorities. Some sequences were even filmed directly from Gr4ves’ CRT, giving the images their wonderfully diseased television texture. “I was trying to embody the spirit of not exactly a dom/sub relationship, but more like a master/servant one,” says Delgado. “This story isn’t romantic in nature, but still has that sweet feeling that the characters do take care of each other. I wanted the Puppet Boy to be not just a “sub,” but rather someone who just doesn’t really know anything else because it’s his whole life–and he has long been fine with this.” The Puppet Boy has no great awakening coming. He knows his place, perhaps enjoys it, and The Phantom Eyes leave him exactly where DEVO put him forty-two years ago: attached to invisible strings, smiling nervously, waiting for somebody else to pull. Watch below: Listen to Puppet Boy below and order the single here. items._cn_summary: 西雅图艺术家The Phantom Eyes以Bex Delgado为核心，对DEVO 1984年专辑Shout中的Puppet Boy进行了暗潮风格的翻唱。与原曲合成器流行喜剧的调性不同，这版将原作的威胁感放大，置入吸血鬼卧室的语境：合成器更冷厉、节奏更具俱乐部驱动力，Delgado以冷静掌控者的声线演唱，使Mothersbaugh原歌词中服从、依赖、情感与所有权的主题获得隐喻层面的情色解读。伴随视频采用CRT失真、VHS降质、红丝绒与肢体接近的视觉语言，营造出80年代地下卡带的污浊魅力。Delgado本人在声明中解释其概念并非严格的主从关系，而是将角色建构为不知其他生活方式的终身依附状态，保留了DEVO原有的反讽基因同时将其推向更黑暗的方向。该作品根植于后朋克与暗潮传统，通过恐怖意象与电子制作重新诠释既有作品。

items.body: Curses Perfect High Altered Circuits Luca Venezia is a tastemaker DJ and producer in the classic mold; via his remixes, curation as the selector behind the superlative Next Wave Acid Punx compilations, and his releases CURSES, the Berlin based artist has been forging a varied, but consistent blend of darkwave, disco, EBM that keeps an eye to the dancefloor but doesn’t skimp on the atmosphere. On Perfect High Venezia digs deep into the new beat and NRG sounds that have informed his work, leaning heavily on funky rhythm programming for grooves. The title track doesn’t waste much time, establishing a big shuffling rhythm accented by orch hits, buzzy synth bass and stabs of sampled guitar to carry the track, its melody limited a simple repeating synth 3 note synth figure and repeated vocals. “Killer Instinct” strips everything down drums and e-bass, much of its texture found in the delay and reverb trails that follow its metallic perc hits and vocal samples. The new beat influence really comes to a head on “Dare 2 Dream”, where a brassy lead flies above pitched and chopped samples and a simple but effect kick-snare pattern, rolling hard at a dancefloor friendly mid-tempo rhythm. CURSES rarely misses, and given how in his wheelhouse Perfect High is, he wasn’t about to start here. Curses – Perfect High EP by Curses Transmigration Living Information self-released London act Transmigration has an immediate rush of nostalgic appeal on recent EP Living Information. Anyone cursorily familiar with electro-industrial will feel immediately at ease with the mix of echoing programming, samples, and vocals which reverberate through the title track or closer “Convergence” – a healthy balance of composition and production ensures that the acid panache of those tracks never oversteps the solid grooves at their base. But spend a bit more time with the EP and you’ll be impressed by how Transmigration’s able to call back to the antecedents of that style as well as bring it into the present without losing their own personality. “Ceaseless” carries a familiarly furtive 242 style forward via the like of Visitor and other modern lo-fi stylists, while the stuttering electro kicks of “Understanding” suggest either Kontravoid or (real heads remember) By Any Means Necessary. That’s a pretty wide historical spread, but Transmigration’s vocal personality as well as their yen for wet, dark electro reverb links those respective points along a thirty-plus year history quite handily. Fun, chewy, and satisfying listening for those who know their history. Living Information by Transmigration The post Observer: Curses & Transmigration appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items._cn_summary: 这张合集聚焦两位当代暗潮电子音乐人的新作。CURSES 在《Perfect High》中深入挖掘新节拍和NRG的律动根基，标题曲以厚重的切分节奏搭配管弦采样、蜂鸣合成器贝斯与吉他切片，旋律克制而聚焦于循环的人声与三音符合成器动机；《Killer Instinct》剥离层次，依赖金属质感的打击与延迟混响残响制造空间感；《Dare 2 Dream》则是新节拍影响的集中呈现，黄铜质主音与处理过的采样在简单的踢镲节奏上翻滚。Transmigration 的《Living Information》以电声工业为基调，呼应Front 242等前辈的同时吸收Visitor、Kontravoid等当代lo-fi制作人的语汇，合成器混响湿润深暗，跨三十余年的风格谱系被其人声特质串联起来。两张作品均在熟悉的类型框架内展现扎实的制作功底与明确的舞池取向。
