items.body: When Side-Line spoke with Rina Pavar in 2023, live performance was still something she approached from outside: the studio was familiar territory, while putting herself physically at the centre of the music remained a challenge. Three years later, watching her open Saturday at Nocturnal Culture Night on the Parkbühne, in daylight and before the festival had fully gathered momentum, the change was striking. The restraint was still there, but it no longer read as self-protection. It had become part of the language. That distinction matters because Pavar’s music is built around control in several senses. She writes, performs, produces and mixes her own material; her arrangements tend towards clarity rather than accumulation; and even live, the electronic architecture necessarily fixes certain parameters in advance. Yet the more interesting development is how she has begun using that control to create freedom rather than insulation. She speaks here about abandoning perfection as a useful measure, learning that a stage persona does not need to be a separate personality, and discovering that authenticity can emerge gradually rather than through some dramatic act of self-reinvention. That makes the timing of this conversation particularly interesting. Her second album, “six”, appeared in March 2025, followed later that year by “REMIXES”, which handed her tightly controlled compositions to artists including Radondo, Kay-Chi, Skelesys, New Haunts and others. In August 2026, “too much” opened another phase: more direct, more emotionally immediate and, in Pavar’s own words, less subtle. Rather than presenting this as a clean break with what came before, she seems more interested in testing how far the existing language can stretch. The final answer she gives here may be the simplest description of that process: think less, be bolder. Rina Pavar interview Karo: I saw you at NCN only a few days ago, on the Parkbühne, and I was thinking about how peculiar the setting actually was for your music: an early festival slot, daylight, people still arriving and adjusting to the day. Does a situation like that require you to construct your own atmosphere almost against the surroundings, or do you prefer not to impose a predetermined mood on a performance at all? Rina: Yes, that was really unusual. But I always take as much time as possible beforehand to rehearse and visualise the specific setting and the audience. I was familiar with NCN and the Parkbühne from a guest’s perspective, so I could easily imagine what my performance would feel and look like at that time. I think this approach allows me to adapt more flexibly to the circumstances, including in my song selection and the style of my performance. Even though, of course, the core always remains the same, the details change with every performance. Karo: When you spoke to Side-Line in 2023, performing was still relatively new territory for you and the studio was very much the place where you felt most secure. Three years later, I watched someone who seemed considerably more settled within the physical act of performing. What changed? Was it simply accumulated experience, or did you have to discover a different version of yourself onstage? Rina: I think it’s a little bit of both. So far, I still don’t approach the unknown entirely without fear or hesitation. That’s why practice and experience remain the cornerstones of my self-confidence and my progress. My stage persona has also changed over time. But through my experiences so far, I’ve realised that there’s actually no need for a “different” version of myself on stage. Rather, as my experience and self-confidence grow, more space opens up for me to enjoy the performance and let my authentic self shine through. That’s why I take the time to discover and refine myself in this environment bit by bit and at my own pace, instead of artificially building something that I’ll eventually have to shed one day because it no longer fits. Karo: “too much” arrived only a few weeks before NCN and has now been presented as the beginning of a new sequence of releases. Why was this particular song the right point of departure? What does it introduce that you felt had not already been said on six? Rina: I think it has a completely different vibe. It’s more direct, more emotional and less subtle in terms of content, without going completely over the top. At least, that’s how I feel about it. That’s why I thought it was the perfect choice for the first single. I’d actually included it in the NCN set, and the reactions were consistently positive. That confirmed my choice. Karo: six contained a great deal of looking backwards: memory, relationships, places, decisions, versions of oneself that have already existed. I wonder whether your writing is changing now from processing experience towards something more immediate. Are you becoming interested in writing from inside an experience while it is still unresolved, rather than only once you understand what it meant? Rina: For me, it always happens in a flexible and spontaneous way. When certain topics or approaches are important to me at the moment, they naturally take centre stage at that time. But things might look completely different again in the next project. Karo: Because you write, perform, produce and mix your own material, almost every important decision remains with you until the mastering stage. That gives you enormous artistic coherence, but presumably also removes the useful resistance another person can provide. How do you recognise the moment when complete creative independence stops being liberating and starts becoming a blind spot? Rina: That’s an important point. And I’ve often had to listen to all the things that can go wrong when you work on your own. That’s why I’ve found the following approach, which works for me. First, I took the pressure off myself to be perfect, and for RINA PAVAR I decided to focus on presenting what comes from me as a person, regardless of whether it’s perfect, good enough, innovative, trendy, cutting-edge or whatever. If it brings me great joy and meets my standards for growth at that moment, then that’s good enough. This creates freedom and keeps me from getting stuck in a safe, rigid framework. Furthermore, with every release, I set new but achievable goals for myself, whether musically, vocally, personally, in live performances or even just in terms of design. I sit down and teach myself something new or try to optimise processes and recognise patterns to eliminate blind spots as much as possible. Karo: There is considerable restraint in your arrangements; individual sounds are often given enough room to become structurally important rather than being surrounded by layers simply because they are available. Is reduction something you consciously work towards? In other words, do you spend as much time deciding what a song can survive without as deciding what it still needs? Rina: I think that’s one of the few things I don’t have to consciously work towards. When I’m producing a song, I actually have to force myself to add elements. I’m always surprised when someone tells me how clean or minimal the mix is. In my mind, I’ve actually “packed it full”, and I often think to myself, “Okay, there’s room for improvement here, and I should be a little bolder in approaching this aspect.” But reduction, or perhaps “clarity” is a better word, is something that runs through everything I do. For me, it’s fulfilling to break down complex situations to their essentials, to distil the core, to organise, structure or simplify things. And that happens completely automatically. Karo: REMIXES placed your songs in the hands of artists with very different instincts, which is almost the opposite of the control you normally have over your work. Was there a remix that revealed something about one of your compositions that you had not recognised yourself, perhaps because another artist emphasised a rhythm, mood or tension that you had considered secondary? Rina: I’d almost say that’s the case with all the songs. Often, my favourite elements are highlighted but placed in a completely different context or emphasised even more. I love every one of these songs and am thrilled to experience my creations in a more developed and reinterpreted form. Karo: Your collaboration with Kay-Chi on “Darkest Night” is interesting for a similar reason, because there you contributed lyrics and vocals to somebody else’s musical framework rather than building the entire environment yourself. Does writing from inside another producer’s world free you in some way, precisely because you are not responsible for every element of the finished piece? Rina: It’s definitely a challenging yet enjoyable situation. I really enjoy not having to take full responsibility for everything. At the same time, though, I often put pressure on myself to do the parts that I work on perfectly. After all, I want to do the song justice and not disappoint the artist who chose me as a collaboration partner. Even though it may seem overwhelming at first, and it’s not always easy to find my place on someone else’s song, I always look forward to projects like this. It’s fun, offers the chance to collaborate and is always a nice change of pace from working solo. Karo: You also work visually, and I am interested less in whether your visual art “matches” the music than in whether the two forms make you think differently. Music unfolds through time, while an image confronts you more or less simultaneously. Does moving between those two ways of organising an idea change the way you compose? Rina: The way I compose doesn’t change because of this. The approaches and the way ideas come to me are simply too different. But painting is my balance to music, and vice versa. For me, it’s a kind of respite from the other and therefore the break I need to develop and bring new ideas to life. Music is often stirring, full of energy and, despite studio work, takes place largely outside. Painting is absolute stillness, tranquillity, grounding and complete isolation from the outside world. Karo: Coldwave and dark electronic music have developed a very recognisable vocabulary, and recognition can become both an advantage and a trap: listeners know immediately where they are, but artists can also end up repeating gestures simply because those gestures belong to the language of the scene. Which elements of that vocabulary still feel central to Rina Pavar, and which ones have you begun questioning? Rina: If I had to name one thing that remains an important, central aspect, or an indispensable element, for me it would be the melancholy in the sound and lyrics. These are still elements of my songs because I’m still drawn to them. But to be honest, I don’t think about genre at all when I’m composing. I create songs based on the premise that “I have to like it” in order to maintain the greatest possible creative freedom. Karo: Electronic performances inevitably contain structures that cannot be altered as freely as they might be in a conventional rock band, yet the person onstage is responding to something entirely unpredictable: an audience. At NCN, how much were you actually reading the people in front of you? Can their response change the way you deliver a song even when its underlying architecture remains fixed? Rina: I can always feel the energy of the audience, and I try to respond to it as best I can. Even though the set is basically fixed, since it’s tied to a tight schedule, especially at a festival like NCN, I still always leave room within that framework to add or omit details, swap out songs, vary my vocal delivery, let loose and adjust the announcements to be longer or shorter depending on how the audience reacts. At NCN, it was great to see that everyone was fully into it even at such an early hour, and that really gave me power. Karo: Your development so far has involved becoming more confident not only as a songwriter but also as someone willing to place herself physically at the centre of the project. At this point, what would artistic growth actually mean to you? Is it greater musical complexity, greater simplicity, taking more emotional risks, collaborating more, reaching larger audiences, or something that has nothing to do with scale at all? Rina: I want to continue acquiring new technical skills and incorporating them into my compositions. When performing live, I’d like to experiment a bit more, both in terms of the performance and the look, as well as the instrumentation. It’s basically a matter of fine-tuning every aspect to bring out and strengthen the essence of RINA PAVAR even more. Karo: Finally, looking ahead: “too much” has been announced as the first of a series of new releases, so we clearly are not looking at an isolated single. Without asking you to reveal anything that should remain a surprise, what is beginning now for Rina Pavar? And when we eventually look back at this next body of work, what do you hope we will hear in it that was not there before? Rina: I do have an idea of what the “new” element will be in the upcoming releases. But since I’m always worried that listeners might not even notice it, I’d like to start by summarising it this way: Think less, be bolder. About Rina Pavar Rina Pavar is a Leipzig-based German solo project started in 2019. Her own Bandcamp describes the music as coldwave and dark electronic music, while Cold Transmission characterises the project through driving basslines, vintage synthesizers, accented vocals and lyrics concerned with consciousness and personal experience. Her debut album, “vivid night”, was released digitally on 1 November 2021, followed by the EP “things we hide” in May 2022. Pavar writes, performs, produces and mixes her own material; those credits are documented on both “vivid night” and her second album. The second album, “six”, was released through Cold Transmission on 21 March 2025. It contains nine tracks and was mastered by Frithjof Rödel at Atomino Studio, with artwork and cover by Pavar and photography by yules_pictures. On 5 December 2025, she released “REMIXES”, a ten-track collection featuring reinterpretations by Radondo, Kay-Chi, Zee Mon, Skelesys, Close Proximity, PJ, Sun’s Spectrum, New Haunts and Three Days Awake by Bent, alongside Pavar’s own club mix of “structured fall”. Pavar also contributed lyrics and vocals to Kay-Chi’s “Darkest Night”, released as part of the Night Protocol EP on 27 March 2026. Her latest single, “too much”, was released on 14 August 2026. Cold Transmission announced it as the first in a series of new releases, marking the beginning of the next phase of the project.
items._cn_summary: 本文为Side-Line杂志对Rina Pavar的专访，围绕她在Nocturnal Culture Night音乐节上的演出展开。乐评指出她的音乐建立在多层面的控制之上：独立完成词曲、演奏、制作与混音，编曲追求清晰而非堆叠，演出中电子架构预先设定参数。然而更值得关注的是她如何将这种控制转化为自由而非隔绝。文章提及她2025年发行的第二张专辑《six》及其后由Radondo、Kay-Chi、Skelesys、New Haunts等艺术家参与的《REMIXES》，以及2026年更具情感直接性的《too much》。她强调放弃完美作为衡量标准，舞台人格无需成为分离人格，真实性可逐步浮现。整篇文字聚焦艺术家创作观念与现场表现的演变，而非具体音乐技术分析。

items.body: Gang of Four, the English post-punk band from Leeds, released their debut album “Entertainment!” on 25 September 1979 through EMI, with Warner Bros. Records handling North America. The album turns 47 this year. It runs 39 minutes and 53 seconds across twelve tracks and was recorded that same year at The Workhouse on the Old Kent Road in London. Jon King and Andy Gill produced it with the band’s then-manager Rob Warr, and Rik Walton engineered. The line-up was King on lead vocals, percussion and melodica, Gill on electric guitar and vocals, Dave Allen on bass and Hugo Burnham on drums. EMI had signed the group after its debut release, the three-track “Damaged Goods” EP, issued on 13 October 1978 by Bob Last’s Edinburgh label Fast Product and recorded at Cargo Studios in Rochdale. Two of those three tracks, “Damaged Goods” and “Love Like Anthrax”, were re-recorded for the album. The running order is “Ether”, “Natural’s Not in It”, “Not Great Men”, “Damaged Goods”, “Return the Gift”, “Guns Before Butter”, “I Found That Essence Rare”, “Glass”, “Contract”, “At Home He’s a Tourist”, “5.45” and “Love Like Anthrax”. King wrote the lyrics under the influence of Situationism, the writing of Michel Foucault and Jacques Lacan, feminism and Marx’s theory of alienation. He also designed the sleeve, which reproduces a still from a Winnetou film in three processed versions, with a text reading: “The Indian smiles, he thinks that the cowboy is his friend. The cowboy smiles, he is glad the Indian is fooled. Now he can exploit him.” “At Home He’s a Tourist” reached number 58 in the UK Singles Chart, still the highest placing of any Gang of Four song. The band were booked to perform it on Top of the Pops, but the producers asked them to change the line “and the rubbers you hide in your top left pocket” to “rubbish”; the group refused and the appearance was cancelled. The album peaked at number 45 on the UK Albums Chart and number 35 in New Zealand. Writing in Rolling Stone in August 1980, David Fricke called it “the best debut album by a British band – punk or otherwise – since the original English release of The Clash”. About Gang of Four Gang of Four formed in Leeds in 1976 around guitarist Andy Gill and singer Jon King, who had met as students. Drummer Hugo Burnham and bassist Dave Wolfson completed the first line-up; after two or three gigs Wolfson was replaced by Dave Allen in 1977. Fast Product released the “Damaged Goods” EP in October 1978, and EMI signed the band the following year. “Entertainment!” arrived in September 1979 and was followed by “Solid Gold” in March 1981 and “Songs of the Free” in 1982, the latter carrying “I Love a Man in Uniform”, which was dropped from BBC playlists during the Falklands conflict. Allen left in 1981 after two albums and went on to co-found Shriekback; Busta “Cherry” Jones filled in before Sara Lee joined as the permanent bassist. Burnham left in 1982 and Steve Goulding took over the drum stool for “Hard” (1983). The band split in 1984. Gill and King reconvened three times in the 1990s, recording “Mall” (1991) with Gail Ann Dorsey on bass and “Shrinkwrapped” (1995). The founding four reunited in 2004 and toured the UK in 2005, releasing the re-recorded “Return the Gift” on 28 September 2005 and performing “Entertainment!” in full for the All Tomorrow’s Parties Don’t Look Back series that year; Side-Line covered the band’s later live material in Exclusive preview Gang Of Four’s ‘Live…In The Moment’ live album. Burnham departed again in late 2005 to return to teaching, and Allen was replaced by Thomas McNeice in 2008. King left in 2011 after disagreements with Gill, and John Sterry took over vocals. That line-up issued “Content” (2011), “What Happens Next” (2015) and “Happy Now” (2019). Andy Gill died on 1 February 2020, aged 64, ending that incarnation of the band. In October 2021 King reformed Gang of Four with Burnham, Sara Lee and Slint guitarist David Pajo for a tour of 1977 to 1983 material. Lee was replaced by Linda Pardee in January 2024 and then by Gail Greenwood that July, and Pajo by Ted Leo in January 2025. Dave Allen died in April 2025, aged 69, having lived with early-onset dementia. The band played its final show in Amsterdam on 6 July 2025. The record’s reach outlasted the band. Die Krupps recorded a version of “To Hell With Poverty” for their 2021 covers album, as reported in Die Krupps cover Gang Of Four with new single ‘To Hell With Poverty’. Michael Stipe has said of the band: “Gang of Four could really swing. I stole a lot from them.” Rolling Stone placed “Entertainment!” at number 490 on its 500 Greatest Albums list in 2003, number 483 in 2012 and number 273 in 2020, and Kevin J. H. Dettmar wrote a book on it for the 33 1/3 series in 2014. Forty-seven years on, the debut remains the album on which the Leeds four-piece set its guitar, bass and drums against lyrics about commodities, contracts and the news.
items._cn_summary: Gang of Four 1979年首张专辑《Entertainment!》由EMI发行，录制于伦敦老肯特路The Workhouse录音室。Jon King与Andy Gill联合制作，融合了情境主义、福柯、拉康、女性主义与马克思异化理论等思想资源，歌词充满批判性张力。专辑仅39分53秒，共十二首曲目，结构紧凑，从《Ether》到《Love Like Anthrax》构建出锐利、去旋律化的吉他语言与紧张节奏。封面由King设计，引用西部片剧照并附以殖民隐喻文字。值得注意的是，《At Home He's a Tourist》因歌词敏感被Top of the Pops拒绝表演。Rolling Stone评价其为英国乐队最佳首张专辑之一。这张作品为后朋克注入了高度概念化与实验性色彩。

items.body: Mondträume is finally back in action with their first new album in seven years. The Spanish band remains driven by Pikotto VondMond, now officially joined by vocalist Nicky Schulschenk (known from N-Frequency). Schulschenk took over from Damasius Venys three years ago and has already featured on the band’s recent EPs. This new album delivers 12 tracks, while the ‘Deluxe Edition’ includes a bonus disc with another 12 songs, comprising additional tracks, remixes, and collaborations. Musically, Mondträume stays true to their infectious, danceable Future-Pop-driven sound. But can we still call it Future-Pop today? Is the genre due for a revival, or is this a kind of ‘Post-Future-Pop’ sound? Ultimately, it doesn’t really matter; the band simply does its own thing, resulting in a polished and complete-sounding album. Danceable rhythms underpin melodies that, devoid of excessive melancholy, come across as cheerful and uplifting. While there are occasional moody passages that provide some variation, the overall production is captivating. Here and there, you’ll notice subtle changes, such as harder, more EBM-oriented basslines, but this is simply part of the genre’s characteristic sound. Previously released tracks such as “Poisoned Love” and, especially, “Pictures Of You” remain fantastic songs that showcase Mondträume at their best. Replacing Damasius Venys was certainly a challenge, but there is clear chemistry between the new duo. Three tracks also feature female vocals by Madril. As mentioned earlier, the bonus disc offers 12 additional tracks, although these aren’t necessarily among my personal favorites. The remixes are the real highlights here, featuring contributions from established remixers such as Rob Dust, while Code 64 and Beyond Border also provide some pleasant surprises. There is even a sort of tribute to Bruderschaft in the form of a remix of “Falling” that Mondträume created some time ago. The ‘Deluxe Edition’ seems primarily aimed at the absolute die-hard fans, but the standard album will undoubtedly attract new listeners as well. Mondträume is back and continues to deliver high-quality Future-Pop. (Rating:8½). Side-Line reported the 2CD announcement for “Mindgames” back in April. Listen to “Pictures Of You”: Pictures Of You by Mondträume About Mondträume Mondträume is a Spanish synth-pop/future-pop duo built around Pikotto Vond Mond. The project released the “The Unknown Path” EP on Alfa Matrix in 2022, followed by the “Heart Machine” EP in 2023 and the “Poisoned Love” single in 2024, before “Mindgames”. Nicky Schulschenk, also known from N-Frequency, took over lead vocal duties from Damasius Venys and discussed the transition in a February 2025 Side-Line interview.
items._cn_summary: 西班牙双人组合 Mondträume 暌违七年推出新专辑《Mindgames》，主创 Pikotto VondMond 与新主唱 Nicky Schulschenk（来自 N-Frequency）合作已三年。专辑收录十二首曲目，豪华版另附十二首加值曲、混音与跨界合作。音乐延续乐队标志性的舞曲化 Future-Pop 路线，旋律明快且不流于过度忧郁，偶有暗色段落穿插以增加层次感。部分曲目加入更偏 EBM 风格的低频线条，预发行单曲「Poisoned Love」与「Pictures Of You」被认为代表乐队最佳状态。女声客串由 Madril 担纲三首。豪华版附碟以 Rob Dust、Code 64、Beyond Border 等混音作品为亮点，并包含向 Bruderschaft 致敬的「Falling」混音版本。整体制作精良、风格统一，属于暗潮/EBM 圈层内的高品质舞曲化合成器流行作品。

items.body: I’m a living god In the same way as all human flesh A pretty song can pose a problem when your band has spent a decade cultivating less agreeable habits. Melbourne quartet Bitumen found themselves facing precisely that predicament with “Perffect Dress,” a handful of chords that had begun behaving suspiciously well. Their response was to introduce a little trouble: vocal distortion, an outlaw-country inflection, and a bouzouki. Beauty survived the intervention, though its manners became considerably less predictable. The single offers an unexpected turn ahead of Reality Red, the band’s third album, due November 6 via It Records. Acoustic instruments and live drums open up fresh possibilities for a group whose post-punk has long accommodated goth, metal, and electronic abrasion. Here, that expansion takes the form of something loose-limbed and oddly pastoral, with a threat tucked into its Sunday best. A slow drum crash and twanging acoustic guitar set the pace, with further strings gathering around the opening figure. There is a country-folk lilt to the arrangement, carried by the easy movement of Andrew Huhtanen McEwan’s drums and Bryce Maher’s bouzouki. As the layers accumulate, a deep bass hum draws the music toward alternative rock and post-punk, while a high electric-guitar line swims through the spaces overhead. The song seems happy to wander, even as its low end keeps track of where everyone is going. Kate Binning’s voice gives that wandering its peculiar charm. Her vocal suggests Marianne Faithfull meets Thom Yorke’s languid reverie. The distortion adds texture without making the performance abrasive; there is an almost whimsical quality to the delivery, a daydream being sung aloud before anyone has checked its contents. Simon Maisch’s murmured backing vocals move beneath her, introducing a second, less easily deciphered train of thought. The words supply ample reason to inspect that daydream. Revenge, freeway exposure, pursuit, and the vulnerability of flesh run through lyrics that keep shifting between smallness and grandiosity. The speaker can be a little sound one moment and a living god the next, claiming divinity on the same terms as every other mortal body. Rearranging a perfect dress becomes a wonderfully incongruous gesture amid all this damage: a small adjustment to one’s appearance while existence itself appears to be coming apart. The overlapping vocal lines complicate the picture further, slipping bodily images and cryptic instructions beneath the lead. The accompanying video places the band around an open fire against corrugated metal, their faces and instruments catching its orange light. Rectangular close-ups overlap the wider performance, bringing hands on strings and Binning’s singing face into the foreground while the gathering continues behind them. As those frames change size and position, the clip moves between collective intimacy and private concentration. It suits the song’s peculiar hospitality: pull up a chair, enjoy the acoustic guitars, and try to overlook the revenge being discussed beside the flames. Watch the video for Perffect Dress below: ﻿ Formed in Melbourne in 2016, Bitumen brings together Kate Binning, Sam Varney, Bryce Maher, and Simon Maisch. Working with a drum machine has been a deliberate part of their approach, allowing guitars, synthesizers, samples, and programmed rhythms to change the terms of each song. On Reality Red, Tongue Dissolver’s McEwan adds live drums to that existing setup, while acoustic instrumentation and a greater openness to melody give the four-piece further room to experiment. Perffect Dress was recorded by Maisch at Lily Street Studios in Coburg North, with McEwan assisting, and produced by the band. Reality Red is available to pre-order here on digital and limited-edition transparent red vinyl through It Records. items._cn_summary: 墨尔本四人组Bitumen在新单曲《Perffect Dress》中进行了意料之外的风格转向，将原声吉他、bouzouki与布祖基琴引入长期以来的后朋克框架，营造出松散而带有乡村民谣气息的质感。贝斯低频沉稳，电吉他高音线游走于空隙之间，层次逐步累积。主唱Kate Binning的声线融合了Marianne Faithfull的沧桑与Thom Yorke的慵懒，失真处理增添肌理而不显粗糙。歌词在复仇、高速公路暴露、追逐与肉身脆弱之间游走，发言人时而自比为微小声音，时而自称活着的上帝，调侃与暴烈并存。MV围绕篝火展开，矩形特写与集体画面交替切换，呼应歌曲内部那种介于亲密聚会与私密沉思之间的张力。该作品预示其第三张专辑在声音维度上将进一步拓展。

items.body: Like many others, my gateway into the Coltrane universe was the inevitable Blue Train , a 1997 CD reissue, with the cover altered with different tones from the original edition. I was beginning to discover jazz and, beyond the variations on the title track, it was the vertigo of “Moment’s Notice” that must have won me over at that early stage. And, of course, the free sound of the saxophone, and the fascinating process of its discourse construction in real time — fascinating for someone who, until then, knew nothing of any form of improvised music. From there, there were several landmark records, in a process that did not follow chronology: it went through the duet with Johnny Hartman, Live at Village Vanguard , the space journey of Meditations , all the way to the devotional magic of A Love Supreme , reading the booklet while following the music, and the pinnacle of Ascension . Along the way, an unavoidable landmark, Giant Steps (as with Ornette’s records, the title also announced the jazz that was coming) with its timeless title track and the melancholic sweetness of “Naima”. I was discovering the albums in no particular order, finding the records or having them find me in a random way, and then gradually organizing Coltrane’s journey in my head, as if piecing a puzzle together. In that process, my favorite album then remains my favorite to this day: My Favorite Things . Too mainstream, too easy, some might say. On ’Trane’s path, a milestone. Not yet the classic quartet, but almost there: McCoy Tyner on piano, Elvin Jones on drums, Steve Davis on bass (Jimmy Garrison would join shortly afterwards). Coltrane takes up the soprano saxophone and transforms a well-known popular melody into a piece of his own; starting from the original melody, he transforms it through a profound process of unfurling. From this point on, it would become one of his signature tunes, evolving into other, much more advanced and deconstructed versions. But this is the start. The LP setlist also has three songs that touch the soul of anyone who loves the history of jazz: one by Cole Porter, “Ev’ry Time We Say Goodbye”, and two by the Gershwins: “Summertime” and “But Not for Me”. In the context of Coltrane's quest and discography, My Favorite Things is a turning point. And, in my own listener's journey, it's music that affects me deeply. Nuno Catarino is editorial coordinator of jazz.pt since 2022. He contributes to the national newspaper Público, where he has written since 2007. He is the author, with Márcia Lessa, of the book Improvisando (2019). Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body: "There is no such thing as a stranger�s children." - old Ukrainian saying I�ve long been affected, indeed somewhat obsessed, by what�s happening in Ukraine, partly because of one of my favorite bands, DakhaBrakha. I went to Kyiv to see them at the time of the Maidan protests, just after the shooting by snipers of over a hundred protesters. I intentionally didn�t read this album�s booklet notes before listening, so that I could react to it without sympathetic pre-judgement, just as music. It�s strong musically and vocally by any standards, Ukrainian or otherwise. When I did then turn to the notes that translate and explain the songs, I had that rare experience, for me, of becoming moist-eyed. The songs are a mix of traditional and original. They are focused on the abduction by Russia of about 20,000 Ukrainian children who have been taken from their parents in Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and sent to Russia, in an attempt to turn them into haters of their native land and people. It�s a heinous war crime. Marichka is a Ukrainian-Canadian singer who moves between Canada and her homeland. For this album she�s gathered two groups of musicians, one in each country. Both ensembles contribute vocals and instrumentation, mostly bowed strings, plus some bandura and piano. The group in Ukraine includes Lisa from the destroyed and invaded city of Mariupol, playing a solo on double ocarina; at 16 she was one of the stolen children but managed to return to Ukraine. Daughters of Donbas � co-led by Marichka and singer/bandurist Alina Kuzma, who shares the lead vocal role � is an all-female ensemble in Canada that tours performing these songs. �Foreign Land� is a reworking of a traditional song about the young girls who were sent away to work in foreign households - Marichka�s grandmother was one of these - that can also be taken to refer to the plight of today�s stolen children. The translation goes: A mother packed up her daughter To leave for a strange land To a strange land with strange people Oh, who will pity you, my daughter? Those who will beat me will pity me I'll never again live with you, my mother When, my daughter, should I expect you to come home? When the grass in the garden grows, my mother The grass grew and grew and began to dry The mother was waiting for her daughter to return, and began to cry Did you hear, my mother, how I came to you? How I flew as a bird above your window? How I cooed like a dove? If, my daughter, I could hear you I would open all the doors and windows To let you fly in Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Alina Kuzma, Zo� Santo As befits the song, Marichka�s vocal here is gentle. But in the second track, �Rusalka,� with Alina Kuzma taking the lead vocals, things turn harsh and fierce. A rusalka is a mythical creature, a nature spirit of fields, forest and rivers, that features in traditional ritual songs. The melody of this one is by Zo� Santo and Kuzma, with lyrics drawing on tradition and the composition of Santo and 19thC Ukrainian poet and folklorist Taras Shevchenko. An ominous double-bass drone, chunking strings, a slithering vocal that moves into sections of white-voice fast recitative and expands into a soaring wild cry. The lyrics are very dark, perhaps evoking the hell of the front line: Home a hell of old growth stumps Marsh a mud of memories Don�t get bogged down in these parts Your kind won�t last a day in here While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. A rusalka sat on a white birch, rusalky asked girls for shirts. Long fingers and nails so sharp Tongue forked round serrated teeth Moss grows down beneath her parts Weeds braided from ear to ear While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. �Girls, my friends, give me your shirts. Though I�m thin, give me a thin one.� Here live us the backless ones Many voices of dead sons You are right to quake in fear Send your sinful children here �Who Am I� is a plea of separation and disorientation, the pain and confusion of an abducted child, contrasting �the human in me� and �the creature in me,� like an internalized riddle-song, with the refrain, in English: Who am I for you? Who am I for me? Do you know me? Really know me? �Enchantress,� passionately sung by Kuzma to her own bandura accompaniment, a girl�s lament of the loss of her brave love taken from her by the enchantress, who is an allegory of war, is based on a traditional song and uses that style of melody and lyrics, �Riddle,� sung by Marichka, reworks a traditional riddle song to be the riddles told by the grandfather of a child, 12-year-old Kira from Mariupol, who experienced the death of her father and her abduction to Russia. Her grandfather tracked her down, and brought her back, traumatized, and asked her riddles - as the notes say �to jog her memory, and remind her who she was, where her home was, and of her family�s love for her.� Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �4.5.0� is a military expression for �all�s well� or �all is quiet.� The song is a message, as from a mother, to a stolen child. Marichka�s voice is cherishing: Remember this: I am with you, I am here Don't give up, I'm with you. Don't give up, I'm with you Your hope is my weapon Don't be sad, I'm with you 4.5.0. will be again �breaking into a tearing howl: And when the world's axis breaks When the sky folds like a parchment Out of nowhere her words will come� �and back to fragile reassurance �It's all right, I'm here, I'm here� "Lullaby," based on a traditional lullaby, sung by Alina Kuzma to accompaniment by her bandura and Zo� Santo's viola, starts in gentle lullaby style, but moves to a lament; it's for the stolen children and those who, as the notes put it, 'have been stolen for ever.' Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �Remember, I Believe in You� is a powerful piece of harmonizing vocals and slithering strings. Here�s the story it�s based on: Yevhen lived in Mariupol with his three young children. During the siege they lived in a basement bomb shelter for months. One day, Russian soldiers entered their bomb shelter. Yevhen was taken to a filtration camp and separated from his children who were all taken to a hospital and then to Russian summer �camp�. In the filtration camp Yevhen was brutally tortured and forced to sleep standing on one leg. He tried to fall asleep, whispering prayers for his children: �Everything will be fine, I believe in you.� After his release he walked 30 kilometers to the place where his children had been taken but it was too late. They had already been sent to Moscow. Yevhen learned of this after receiving a text from one of his children who had found an unattended device. He traveled thousands of kilometers, crossed the borders of three countries, endured checks, interrogations and danger to reach Moscow and take his children home. All those days he tirelessly repeated to himself, �I believe in myself, I believe in my kids. Everything will be good.� �Another Heaven,� sung by Marichka with the ensemble in Ukraine, is inspired by another heart-rending story: Ilya was 9 years old when his mother was killed by a rocket strike right in front of him. He was taken to a hospital in occupied Donetsk, where 15 pieces of shrapnel were removed from his body without anesthesia. After he appeared in a report on Russian television, Ilya�s grandmother learned his location. She managed to bring her grandson to Kyiv, where he lives now, experiencing missile attacks every night. At age 11, he says that it is up to everyone to fight enemies, to protect other cities, and to build another heaven, where your home will not be destroyed. In 2014, during the Kyiv Maidan protests, Marichka wrote and performed �Red Boots Tango,� using a melody she�d put to a poem by Taras Shevchenko. For this album she sings it again in Ukraine, with the ensemble there adding swirling, classic tango-style strings. Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, BanduraGirl The final track on the album is a solo, recorded in Kyiv, by Anastasiya Voytyuk, accompanying herself on the older, simpler form of bandura that was used by kobzars to accompany epic poetry, and also on the nowadays more well-known big, heavy form developed from it in Soviet times that was made mainly in the piano factory at Chernihiv. Her song, �Soon I Will Be Back,� is based on a poem by novelist, journalist and war crime researcher Victoria Amelia, who was killed in 2023, in the city of Kramatorsk in Donbas, by a Russian rocket. Find the artist online. Further reading: Otava Yo - Do You Love (Review) Sofia Rei - Umbral (Review)

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑聚焦俄罗斯占领区约两万名被强制带离父母的乌克兰儿童，以传统与原创歌曲交织的方式呈现这一战争罪行。乌克兰裔加拿大歌手Marichka联合两国乐手录制，器乐以弓弦乐器为主，辅以班杜拉琴、钢琴与双陶笛，音乐质地丰富。歌词层面，《异乡》取材传统叙事，描述少女被送往陌生之地劳作的历史记忆，与当代被夺走儿童的命运形成呼应；《Rusalka》则取材斯拉夫民间传说中的水泽仙女传统，旋律转向粗粝激烈。女声和声在克制与锋利之间切换，既承载文化记忆，也直面当下苦难，将民族伤痛转化为声音文本。

items.body:
According to its founder, Eugene Rodriguez, who also sings and plays on the record, Los Cenzontles is a �musical group and non-profit organization, which I founded over thirty years ago.�  As he continues in the album�s liner notes, the group �has a long history of producing projects exploring Mexico�s deep roots and our connections with various traditions that, so far, have included Irish, Louisiana Creole, Cuban, American cowboy, classical, pop, rock, and blues�, the latest of which is
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
. Los Cenzontles translates to the mockingbird, or, from its Aztec root word, the bird of four hundred voices. This is a fitting name for the range of musical diversity represented here.
With songs sung in Spanish, Hawaiian, and English, the concept traces back to the legacy of Mexican cowboys who travelled from California to the Hawaiian Islands to wrangle the long-horned cattle introduced there in the nineteenth century. They also brought the guitar. The 16 tracks feature old Hawaiian songs with new Spanish lyrics, old Mexican songs with new Hawaiian lyrics, new compositions, and traditional Americana. Yet it is an entirely cohesive musical package held together by dense arrangements of ukuleles, guitars, Mexican harp, and accordion.
Sonny Lim & David Hidalgo
Besides their distinctive voices, the headline artists Taj Mahal and David Hidalgo provide the gravitas and musicianship that their long and distinguished careers have earned. According to the liner notes, they were the catalysts behind the project and facilitated the choice of songs, arrangements, and played a range of instruments. On vocals they are joined by Hawaiian natives Gary Haleamau, Sheldeen Haleamau, Sonny Lim, and long-time Cenzontles member Fabiola Trujillo.
Deportee
To give a taste of the sessions, included before the traditional �Fishin� Blues� is Taj Mahal teaching the musicians how to play it. Sung by David Hildalgo,  the lovely �A Matter of Time� comes from the 1984 album
Will the Wolf Survive
by his most famous project, Los Lobos. Another standout for me, �Navegar� features a slack string guitar solo reminiscent of Duane Eddie and one of many tasty lap steel turns by Sonny Lim. Their interpretation of Woody Guthrie's �Deportee� moves into social commentary, highlighting the cruel realities of being a migrant worker in America.
Vaquero Paniolo
Recorded over five days, mostly live in one room at the Los Cenzontles headquarters in San Pablo, California, including the talents of some of their academy�s students, the recording has real spontaneity to it. Arrangements are stretched by improvisations, sometimes by several different instruments on a single tune. The project also represents a great spirit of cooperation and diversity of language, culture, age, and gender. It includes the inputs of musical legends, seasoned pros, and amateurs. The wonderfully rich and often stereotyped musical cultures of both Mexico and Hawaii are represented here with the authenticity of lived experience.
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
is a worthy addition to Los Cenzontles� important work. Quoting Rodriguez again, �Culture is a fabric within which we are all woven.�

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由一位瑞典小提琴家与两位挪威乐手组成三重奏，演奏源自斯堪的纳维亚传统舞蹈曲调。三位音乐人长期致力于模糊不同音乐流派之间的界限，跨越挪威与瑞典民间音乐界线，并融入萨克斯风、风笛等非传统乐器。专辑采用非常规方式重新演绎传统舞曲，将其转化为类似室内乐的质感：三位乐手沉浸在亲密的音乐对话中，探索旋律中隐藏的意义可能性，揭示表面欢快之下的暗流与神秘感。小提琴家马茨·埃登提供纹理化的伴奏层，长笛手特莱夫·奎夫特主领旋律线条，鼓手克努特·奎夫特·内斯海姆以轻敲细碎的节奏点缀。乐评特别以挪威塞特斯达尔地区的民间传说为切入点，将音乐与易卜生戏剧中表面温情下潜伏的不安相类比，营造出萦绕于北欧传统的幽暗氛围。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Logos channels a classic Gothic symphonic rock sound; the use of synthesizers and keyboards in "Origami in SOL" serves as an introduction to a complex musical tapestry reminiscent of Metamorfosi, particularly in "Paesaggi di insonnia," a track that borders on psychedelia through its juxtaposition of keyboard layers. The spirit of Genesis, combined with the saxophone, creates a dense atmosphere that nonetheless flows effortlessly, thanks to a dark, epic jazz influence, driven by a powerful underlying purpose: this is a concept album about the life of Sadako Sasaki. She was a Japanese girl who was two years old at the time of the nuclear attack on Hiroshima; she later fell ill and passed away at the age of twelve. This story gave rise to the Japanese legend of the thousand paper cranes (origami) that Sadako attempted to fold in the hope of recovering.The track's frenetic pace in Un lieto inquietarsi, is comparable to Le Orme's magnum opus, Felona e Sorona; the interplay between the drums, keyboards, and synthesizer weaves a musical tapestry that sets the stage for various solos, while an ominous aura gradually takes hold, including a decidedly non-festive use of the Hammond organ.Shifts in tempo occur naturally, amidst the abruptness with which the music bursts forth, drawing upon the full majesty of the classical repertoire, where Baroque polyphony paves the way for Luca Zerman's vocals, which adapt seamlessly to the context. In Il Sarto one notices the resemblance of Luca Zerman's voice to Aldo Tagliapietra (from Le Orme) and then he is joined by Elisa Montaldo, pianist and singer of the progressive band Il Tempio Delle Clessidre, in a great and emotional duet."Zaini di Elio" begins with the feel of 1970s Genesis, specifically the Phil Collins era, before allowing itself to be captivated by the structures of J.S. Bach; combined with Alessandro Perbellini's drumming, the music takes on the quality of a dance alongside the electric clavichord. It evokes Tony Banks and Phil Collins during the ...And Then There Were Three... period, though the sound drifts toward a more pastoral atmosphere, incorporating traditional vocal elements from the artist's native Verona. The layering of the various keyboard lines is so delicate that the transitions are imperceptible: it sounds as though the music had always been there.Sadako e le mille gru di cartareminds me of Hiroshima Mon Amour, Alain Resnais's film, and the subtlety of addressing such a subject with poetry and respect; stepping back to draw closer from a different angle, the kind of perspective only the passage of time can provide. Here, Claudio Antolini's piano takes on a new depth, and the rhythm that has driven the album pauses. Musical passages evoke Eastern melodies, telling the story through sound, accompanied by ghostly-sounding Minimoog emulations. Never before has a folded sheet, a crumpled scrap of paper, held so many layers of meaning or interpretation. The music provides the accompaniment: dramatic, yet also epic and inspiring, conveying a strength that rises from the ashes. Driven by keyboards and drums, the composition blends classical elements with syncopated rhythms, building toward an operatic finale as the paper figure unfolds, a symbol of the hope that nothing happens in vain, even if it seems otherwise at the time. That was precisely the hidden meaning behind the twists and intersections of the music itself.
items._genre: rock progressivo italiano / gothic symphonic rock / progressive rock
items._cn_summary: Logos 的这张概念专辑围绕广岛核爆幸存者佐佐木禎子的真实故事展开，将巴洛克复调、东亚旋律元素与意大利前卫摇滚传统相融合。评论者重点指出合成器键盘的层次编织、Hammond 风琴的非喜庆运用，以及 Luca Zerman 的声线与 Aldo Tagliapietra 的相似性。专辑在 Genesis 式的氛围铺陈与 Le Orme 式的紧凑叙事之间切换，Minimoog 模拟音色与东方旋律交汇于叙事核心。Dramatic 的节奏转换和古典语汇的引用为作品增添厚度，使其超越了单纯的复古模仿，呈现出对历史悲剧的诗意追忆。整体而言，乐评展现了较高的写作质量，但作品风格更偏向传统前卫摇滚范畴，与用户偏好的实验、前卫、当代古典融合方向存在一定距离。

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — For the most part early 70s German Krautrock morphed into the more instrumentally demanding Krautjazz fusion that found a rather sizable following in the second half of the decade when prog ingeneral had declined. Some bands though found a nice middle ground between the heady koschmischevibes of the space age and placed them alongside the more focused workouts of the jazz fusion scene.One such band was MORPHEUS that was spawned from an earlier band called Opossum which existed from1971 to 1975 but was never successful at releasing its own material although an archival releasewould see the light of day decades later in 2003. While Opossum was a more free form jazz kinda Kraut, a couple members wanted to play more psych-soaked structured tracks in the vein of other German fusion acts such as Kraan and Missus Beastleyor Embryo for that matter. The results was the short-lived MORPHEUS from Warburg that existed fortwo years from 1975 to 1977 and released its one and only album RABENTEUER smack dab in the middleof its career in 1976. Far from free form, MORPHEUS gathered grooves from the world of prog rock,trippy effects from the Kraut scene and more accessible jazz stylings also from the German scene.The result was a nicely displayed album that rocked, was smothered in jazz and offered a moresubdued heady vibe courtesy of spacey effects and a sensual flautist on board.Another of the many rarities that were generated during the era, RABENTEUER was limited to 500copies and went undiscovered until the Garden of Delights label resurrected the album for a 1998 CDrelease. Steeped in psych-fueled jazz rock, RABENTEUER features six all-instrumental tracks thatoffer funk-fueled bass grooves, gnarled workouts that offer labyrinthine structured compositions toflow around a rather accessible compositional flair only fortified with complex soundscapes,bountiful helpings of time signature deviations and ample doses of soloing between the variousmusicians that consisted of Peter Bl�meke (bass, flute), Gerold Adler (guitar), Heinrich Holtgreve(alto saxophone) and Alfred Franke (drums). While the tracks are primarily upbeat and more in thejazz rock camp, "Tanz Der Morphine" takes a dive into the space rock world of koschmische Kraut.Like many of the similarly minded bands of the era, MORPHEUS delivered the chops as far as jazz-infused prog was concerned with nice accessible hooks augmented by the more complex attributes ofthe words of both prog and fusion however the album as competently performed as it is sounds a bitlike those same similarly minded acts that didn't really add a lot to the world of jazz fusion atthis stage in the game. The tracks are pleasant but almost by the books in approach without any realfiery passion emerging by the rather consistent display of instrumental interplay. Overall it's anice supplemental piece from the era but not one that strikes me as utterly essential either.Pleasant but not much else. The CD version offers an extra long 20-minute jam track but this is evenof less interest than the album in general.3.5 rounded down
items._genre: krautrock / jazz fusion / prog rock / krautjazz
items._cn_summary: MORPHEUS 是1975至1977年间活跃于德国Warburg的短命乐队，前身为Opossum。其唯一专辑《RABENTEUER》于1976年发行，仅限量500张，至1998年由Garden of Delights厂牌以CD形式再版。乐队融合了德国Krautrock的迷幻氛围、爵士融合的器乐律动与进步摇滚的复杂结构，六首纯器乐曲目由贝斯兼长笛手Peter Blömke、吉他手Gerold Adler、中音萨克斯手Heinrich Holtgreve与鼓手Alfred Franke共同完成。作品以放克贝斯线条为主轴，辅以迷宫式的复合节拍变化与即兴solo段落，长笛与空间音效赋予作品朦胧的太空感，其中'Tanz Der Morphine'偏向Kosmische氛围。乐评指出乐队演奏技艺扎实，但整体风格与同期Kraan、Missus Beastley、Embryo等德式融合乐队过于接近，未带来显著突破，虽属时代佳品但非不可或缺之作。

items.body: The Actions, a Bristol alt-electronic duo, released the single and video “Container” on 25 September 2026 through the Barcelona label No Where Records. The track is the first single from an album the duo have set for spring 2027, following their March 2026 single “Take More.” “Container” is also available to stream on Spotify. ‘Container’ marks The Actions’ first single since ‘Take More’ No Where Records describes “Container” as pushing the duo’s blend of “alternative electronics, dark textures and powerful songwriting” further than their previous single. The Actions describe themselves as an alt-electro-noise duo, and their recent work blends rock and electronic music with a punk-like directness, a shift they trace back to the March 2026 single “Take More.” About The Actions The Actions are a Bristol duo made up of Marta Argenio, who also performs as Silty, and Maurizio “Mo” Stellato. The pair share vocal, guitar and bass duties alongside electronics, exploring the space between rock and electronic music. Their debut album, “Flourish,” came out in 2021. The duo have previously opened for R.E.M., Green Day, Garbage and The Distillers, and earned airplay on BBC Radio 6 Music. The Actions returned in March 2026 with “Take More,” a three-track single pairing the original with a stripped-back “Flatland Mix” and a remix from IKO Twins, backed by a music video Mo edited through his own MStar Design work. The band said the record marked a turn toward something stronger and more direct than their earlier, more atmospheric work: “After our last, more transcendent record, we felt the urge to return with something stronger and more direct, and though it took time to get there, we knew this was the right moment to come back.” They called it “a song about growing up in the suburbs,” weighing whether to stay with the people they love or break away. The Actions joined No Where Records in July 2026. “Container” is the duo’s first release for the Barcelona label and the opening single from the album they have scheduled for spring 2027.
items._cn_summary: The Actions是来自布里斯托尔的二人组合，成员Marta Argenio与Maurizio Stellato在电子与摇滚的交汇地带创作，自2021年首张专辑《Flourish》以来持续探索另类电子、暗黑质感与直接有力的歌曲结构之间的张力。2026年3月单曲《Take More》标志着他们从早期氛围化作品转向更具冲击力的方向，2026年9月通过巴塞罗那独立厂牌No Where Records发行的《Container》延续了这一路线，被厂牌描述为在另类电子、暗黑音色与歌曲创作之间的融合上比前作走得更远。两人共享人声、吉他与贝斯与电子声部，此前曾为R.E.M.、Green Day、Garbage及The Distillers暖场，并在BBC Radio 6 Music获得播放。《Container》作为2027年春季专辑的首支先行单曲，展示了他们在电子与摇滚融合层面的持续推进。

items.body: Brazilian vocalist Anna Vis and Príncipe label affiliate Helviofox are among the artists playing next year's event Anna Vis SQUARE festival has revealed the first wave of acts playing its 2027 edition in January. The Portuguese festival returns to its main base of Braga for its third year, with additional programming set to spread out to nearby Northern Portugal bases of Famalicão, Guimarães and Viana do Castelo. The lineup has been put together by SQUARE's organisers, and its network of festival and events partners, such as Iceland Airwaves, MENT, Rewire, Nyege Nyege and Novas Frequências. The theme of next year's SQUARE will be Continuity, and this will explore "the projects that endure, the acts of care and repair that sustain them, and the people and structures that keep independent... items.body: Godflesh Decay A pummelling swan song from the legendary industrial metal powerhouse Decay by GODFLESH Bands heralding their own end is not that uncommon a thing. Godflesh themselves have done this twice so far. But it hits differently when it’s a cherished band from your late adolescence. The Brummie duo were, for me, an epiphanic trove unearthed around the time of their reunion, shaping my taste for the heavy, low-tuned and minimalist strains of extreme music amid the ruins of what could once have been an independent, DIY, creative, intrepid scene, long since lost. But this time, it seems to be for good, and the dismantling of Godflesh’s machinery has been set in motion by Justin Broadrick, the act’s main driving force, whose inability... The post Godflesh – Decay appeared first on The Quietus.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑被描述为工业金属传奇乐队的谢幕之作，承载着终结意味。乐评者将这支双人乐队视为青少年晚期的重要发现，其低频调弦与极简主义风格塑造了自身对极端音乐的审美取向。专辑延续乐队标志性的沉重、机械化声响路径，强调反复碾压式的节奏与金属质感的工业肌理。文中透露出这是乐队主脑再次启动解散程序的信号，乐评带有强烈的个人情感投射，回忆了独立与DIY场景曾经存在的语境。整体定位为工业金属范畴内偏实验与极端走向的作品，介于主流金属与地下实验之间，文章提供了个人化的聆听语境但缺乏对具体声响技法的深入剖析。

Before discussing *La Scienza delle Stagioni*, Andrea Orlando's second album, it might be helpful to review the following preliminary points:1. The Bands. Andrea Orlando is the drummer on all four albums by La Coscienza Di Cena, an RPI band founded in Genoa in 2007, which released a superb self-titled debut album in 2011 and three other highly recommended albums between 2013 and 2018. Is it worth noting here that Genoa (Genova) is the birthplace of the illustrious PFM, one of the founding fathers of Italian progressive rock (RPI)?Before the formation of La Coscienza Di Cena, Andrea Orlando had already gained some recognition in this microcosm as a member of what it's fair to call the "Zuffanti nebula"?a transalpine prog music collective that began to coalesce around the Genoese bassist Fabio Zuffanti in the early '90s and gained greater visibility with Finisterre's debut album (1995).2. The Artist. Andrea Orlando joined Finisterre as early as 1997 on their *Live at Progday* and then on the fabulous *In Ogni Luogo* (1999), before returning for the 2019 comeback album. Orlando also played drums on *Mirrogames* (1998) by H�stsonaten, Zuffanti's other major band. In both cases, Orlando replaced Marco Cavani. To round out this overview, it's worth noting that drummer Andrea Orlando also contributed to the album by La Curva di Lesmo (2015), a duo that Zuffanti formed with Stefano Agnini, one of the two keyboardists on La Coscienza. And that brings us partially full circle.Let's now turn to the album itself by going over the other two points:3. The musicians. Since Andrea Orlando is one of the stalwarts of this famous Genoese music scene, it's no surprise that for his two solo albums, he called on other members of that same scene. For example, to give credit where credit is due, Zuffanti himself plays bass on one track from *La Scienza delle Stagioni*, and Boris Valle (Finisterre's longtime keyboardist) plays piano on another. Orlando, an accomplished drummer but also a capable keyboardist (with a predilection for the mellotron and organ), here cedes the piano parts?in addition to Valle?to Luca Scherani (H�stsonaten, La Coscienza di Zeno, La Curva di Lesmo) and to Agostino Marco (Finisterre, La Maschera, Zaal) for the Moog solos.On *Dalla Vita Autentica*, Andrea Orlando's previous solo album, the majority of the electric guitar parts were performed by two highly talented musicians: Marcella Arganese?who can be found in Ubi Maior and who regularly dazzles us with *Samura� of Prog*?and Laura Marsano, whom we've seen on Zuffanti's solo albums and those of drummer Maurizio Di Tollo. Two women on guitar?and not just any women?is rare enough to be worth noting, whatever the critics of "wokism" may say. On *La Scienza delle Stagioni*, Marcella has been replaced by Stefano Marelli, but Laura Marsano is always there to treat us to her poignant solos (the slow "Stagione Lontana"). The young singer Meghi Moschino contributes her calm, medium-toned voice to five of the seven tracks?a voice that reminds me a bit of Laura Mombrini's (Prowlers). On *Dalla Vita Autentica*, the robust vocals of Alessandro Corvaglia (another essential, ubiquitous figure on the RPI scene for several years), paired with those of Simona Angioloni (remember *Aries*, the band formed in the 2000s with? Zuffanti, him again), gave the whole a more robust feel. A matter of taste.4. The music. *La Scienza delle Stagioni* alternates between dynamic, vibrant tracks rooted in PFM's sun-drenched RPI, and tenderly romantic moments that unfold into expansive, emotionally charged symphonic prog, closer in style to *Hostsonaten*. By elegantly blending these two styles, the diptych "Il Sogno di Anastasia" (12:12) stands out as one of the album's most compelling tracks. In addition to "Il Sogno di Anastasia ? Parte Seconda," a lovely musical reverie with enchanting undertones, the album includes another instrumental, "City 40" (6:36), a sort of high-energy Latin version of "Samurai of Prog."The influence of Camel, noticeable from the very start of the previous album ("Le Forme Della Distanza"), is less pronounced throughout *La Scienza delle Stagioni*, giving way to more personal ideas, resulting in a kind of symphonic neo-prog with strong RPI influences. On the other hand, the extensive and frequent use of the mellotron (the long intro to "Stagione Lontana" with its celestial tones, or that of "La Strada del Ritorno," among others) draws the most serene moments toward the most ethereal Scandinavian prog.Of roughly similar length, the epic closing track, the highly symphonic "La Strada del Ritorno" (15:01), can be compared to the thrilling "Dalla Vita Autentica" (16:52), which closed the 2017 album of the same name, illuminated by an unforgettable solo by Marcella Arganese. But despite some structural and musical similarities, the comparison ultimately favors the latter, which is more ambitious and features more inspired melodies. Yet the melancholy that envelops the final section of "La Strada del Ritorno"?enhanced by Meghi's angelic voice and the serene appearance of the English and French horns?ultimately moves us, giving us the impression that a pale winter sun has come to breathe its loving breath upon us.At first glance, *La Scienza delle Stagioni* seems a little less striking than its predecessor, *Dalla Vita Autentica*. At the very least, it builds on its predecessor's strengths while retaining all its qualities, though without reaching quite the same heights. But let's not be fooled by first impressions. There are prog albums that possess a kind of natural clarity, made up of music whose beauty is immediately apparent; and others, like *La Scienza delle Stagioni*, that save their magic for a little later, revealing it just after we've finished listening, when we think we've moved on to something else. But that is the secret art of these mysterious works: to prepare for us an immediate future more beautiful than expected. *La Scienza delle Stagioni* possesses that special magic that fairies bestow as they lean over the cradle of certain works?a magic that stays with you and illuminates your path long after the notes have faded away.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由热那亚鼓手Andrea Orlando作为个人项目的第二张作品，围绕四季主题展开。文章重点介绍了作者的背景脉络：他长期活跃于意大利前进摇滚圈层，参与过La Coscienza di Zeno、Finisterre、Höstsonaten等多个乐队，并与Genova音乐场景的核心人物Fabio Zuffanti有密切合作。专辑邀请了同一圈的乐手参与，如Zuffanti本人演奏贝斯、Finisterre键盘手Boris Valle弹钢琴，以及多位客座吉他手。作品延续了七十年代意大利前进摇滚的语法框架，运用mellotron、organ、Moog合成器等键盘音色，女吉他手的solo段落构成情感亮点。整体属于对RPI传统较为忠诚的延续性创作，在旋律和器乐编排上保持该类型典型特征，但在声音探索或跨领域融合方面未有明显突破。

items.body: Review by greenpete — They made a startlingly confident beginning with their exuberant, minor-label debut, An Evening With Dando Shaft (no, not a live album). But Dando Shaft's high-water mark arrived with this, their sophomore LP (often called the "Carousel" album, and released on RCA's short-lived Neon label, which only issued 11 albums total). This record dispenses entirely with drums, plunging deeper into varied, lyrical progressive folk. Singer Polly Bolton, from the wonderfully named village of Leamington Spa, joined the boys to bolster their string intricacies with her breathy, Sandy Denny-esque voice. The debut was marred only by the awkward "The Cat Song," but on the Carousel album, there's really not a bad cut. The Bulgarian-rhythmic songs of dual guitarists Dave Cooper and Kevin Dempsey, and mega-instrumentalist Martin Jenkins, are consistently strong, with Jenkins' mandolin, flute, and fiddle shining here. His tune "Whispering Ned," about a gent who enjoys indulging in sugar cubes (and whom the band evidently knew) adds an imaginative twist to the canon of drug songs. The upbeat "Pass it On" is notable for its exuberant chorus about values that have, sadly, since gone out of style. But the real highlights are "Till the Morning Comes" and "River Boat." Both feature Bolton's angelic vocals, the former a wispy duet with Cooper graced by luscious, gently psychedelic flute (Jenkins) and tablas (Ted Kay); and the latter an utterly breathtaking, pastoral delight that conjures green, rural England in poem-song.Bolton would stick around for Lantaloon, a good but inessential album, then depart after tiring of feeling like a "guest" vocalist. So if you plan to only get one album by this highly underappreciated psych-folk band...take a ride on the Carousel.- greenpete
items._cn_summary: 这是英国乐队Dando Shaft的第二张专辑，被乐评视为其巅峰之作。专辑完全舍弃鼓的运用，由两把吉他、曼陀林、长笛与提琴构建层次丰富的民谣织体。女主唱Polly Bolton的声线轻柔空灵，赋予作品浓郁的英式田园气质。乐评特别提及融合保加利亚节奏的吉他编排，以及塔布拉鼓与迷幻长笛的对话，呈现出一定的跨界实验色彩。歌词方面既有暗指毒品的趣味叙事，也有探讨价值观的合唱段落。整体而言，这是一张制作精良的民谣专辑，在传统英伦民谣框架内融入了少量东方节奏与前卫编曲意识，但对追求实验性、先锋性或即兴深度的听众而言，融合程度仍偏保守。

items.body: Soft Riot has finished a video for “Ghostwriter,” the closing track on the 2026 album “Crux.” It is the project’s second official video from the record, following “Moving Out Of The Black,” which premiered at the end of April 2026 ahead of the album’s release on 15 May. A premiere date for “Ghostwriter” itself is still being finalised; the video is not yet public. Crux by Soft Riot Jack Duckworth, who records as Soft Riot and is also known as JJD, built the video’s visuals as a graphic, surrealist collage rather than a straight performance piece, with puppet-like character animation reflecting the song’s theme: the sense of ideas for “Crux” materialising, as though something unseen were “ghostwriting” the record. All of the animation was made by hand from physically printed graphics and re-filmed projected textures, a deliberate move away from computer-based tools that Duckworth has linked to feeling increasingly isolated within the digital side of underground music. Duckworth handled all graphics and editing as JJD, with assistance from Leyre Mann Vadillo. “Ghostwriter” closes a nine-track album written and recorded across several sessions between June 2024 and January 2026 at Studio Carillon in Glasgow, with vinyl mixing by Owen Pratt at Flesh And Bone Studios in Tarn, France, and mastering by Josh Stevenson at Otic Mastering. “Crux” is available on streaming platforms, as a download through Bandcamp and Subvert via Possession Records, and on vinyl and digipak CD, including a limited clear vinyl LP on Minimal Kombinat that sold out within a week of pre-orders. A follow-up EP, “Alter,” released in June 2026, carries exclusive, alternate and extended versions of “Crux” material. About Soft Riot Soft Riot is the synth project of Jack Duckworth, a British-Canadian musician based in Glasgow who has released music under the name for around fifteen years, drawing on synth post-punk, darkwave, new wave, Italo and EBM. Duckworth’s roots go back to the mid-1990s art-punk and hardcore scene on the North American west coast, where he played in the first-wave post-punk revival band Radio Berlin (1998-2005) and the industrial synth-punk group A Luna Red (Gold Standard Labs, 1999-2003). As Soft Riot, he has toured Europe repeatedly, sharing stages with acts including Front 242, Absolute Body Control, Parade Ground, She Past Away, Test Department, Selofan, Drab Majesty and Lebanon Hanover, and has played festivals including Ombra Festival in Spain, BIM Fest and Waveteef in Belgium, Kalabalik På Tyrolen in Sweden and Weird Science in Germany. Side-Line has previously covered the Soft Riot albums “You Never Know What Might Come Next” (2016), “The Outsider In The Mirrors” (2018) and “When Push Comes To Shove” (2019), followed by “No.” (2023) and, in 2026, “Crux” and its “Alter” companion EP.

items.body: Front Line Assembly released their eighth studio album, “Hard Wired,” through Off Beat on 25 September 1995, with Metropolis Records handling North America and Energy Rekords issuing the record in Sweden. It was the Canadian electro-industrial band’s first release for the German label. The album turns 31 this year. Bill Leeb and Rhys Fulber produced the record and wrote all ten tracks, which run 62 minutes: “Neologic Spasm,” “Paralyzed,” “Re-Birth,” “Circuitry,” “Mortal” (instrumental), “Modus Operandi,” “Transparent Species,” “Barcode,” “Condemned” and “Infra Red Combat.” Greg Reely engineered and mixed, with Delwyn Brooks assisting, continuing a working partnership that began on “Caustic Grip” in 1990. Devin Townsend played electric guitar, returning after his session work on the previous year’s “Millennium.” Dave McKean produced the illustration, design and photography. The sessions ran roughly five months at the Warehouse. Leeb wrote the lyrics only once the music was finished, and described that order as the band’s normal method rather than a choice made for this record: “We write […] the music and then once we’ve got it finished, then I sit at home and start on the lyrics. I can’t imagine writing any other way. […] I think with our music it’s usually the sounds that inspire us.” On what those lyrics deal with, he set materialism and environmental collapse against the technology driving both: “I think most of the lyrics are basically about man versus technology. Basically, we’re destroying our planet with technology. At the same time, technology is the only thing that can save us. It’s this constant struggle between these two forces that is making us go in whatever direction we’re all going.” That reading runs through the sampling as well. The album draws audio from “True Romance,” “In the Mouth of Madness,” “Lifeforce,” “Stargate,” “Speed,” “The Puppet Masters,” “No Escape,” “Romeo Is Bleeding,” “The Crow,” “Lethal Weapon” and “Alien 3,” alongside sound effects from the 1993 video game “Doom” and passages from three Aphex Twin recordings. “Circuitry” was the album’s only single, released on 31 October 1995. Its limited edition came as a two-CD digipak with remixes by Haujobb and Biosphere, a mixed-mode first disc carrying the “Millennium” video and photo galleries, and a second disc with the non-album tracks “Destructive Transformation” and “Hydrogen.” The album reached number 47 on the Swedish albums chart and the single number 32 on the Swedish singles chart. “Hard Wired” has sold at least 50,000 copies worldwide, and its 5,000-copy limited edition sold out in two weeks. A further track from the same sessions, “Plasticity,” was held back and issued separately; Fulber explained the decision in commercial terms: “We kept it off the album to release later […] It gives people a reason to check it out because if you release it as a single that is already on album no one is really going to care.” The “Plasticity” video won Best Alternative Video at the MuchMusic Video Awards in Toronto in 1996. The album has returned to shelves twice since. Black Rain Records pressed a 500-copy picture vinyl in August 2011, cut to seven songs, dropping “Mortal,” “Modus Operandi” and “Transparent Species.” For the record’s twentieth year, Artoffact Records issued a 300-copy vinyl box in 2015 pairing the album with the “Live Wired” live record and the “Circuitry” single, all remastered by Reely; Side-Line reported that The Front Line Assembly 6LP boxset ‘Hard Wired’ is almost sold out that May, and covered the same year’s news that Front Line Assembly finally see ‘Plasticity’ released on a 10 inch vinyl (3 formats). “Hard Wired” streams on Spotify. About Front Line Assembly Bill Leeb formed Front Line Assembly in Vancouver, Canada, in 1986, shortly after leaving Skinny Puppy, where he had contributed bass synth and backing vocals between 1985 and 1986 under the name Wilhelm Schroeder. He picked the band name to reflect his view that strength lies in working together. The demo tapes “Nerve War” and “Total Terror” were limited to 100 copies each and mostly passed around among friends, with Rhys Fulber contributing as an unofficial member. The project’s first appearance on record was “Aggression,” on the 1987 Third Mind compilation “For Your Ears Only.” Belgian label KK issued the debut album “The Initial Command” at the end of 1987, with Fulber and Michael Balch assisting, and German label Dossier released “State of Mind” in January 1988. When a planned Nettwerk release fell through, Third Mind put out “Corrosion” and the “Disorder” EP later that year, then signed the band to a three-album deal and licensed “Corrosion” to Wax Trax! for North America. Balch became an official member in 1988 and left after the 1989 “Gashed Senses & Crossfire” tour to join Ministry and Revolting Cocks. Fulber replaced him and appeared on “Caustic Grip” (1990), the album that started the band’s long partnership with engineer Greg Reely and introduced guitar on “Provision” and “Resist.” Chris Peterson debuted as live percussionist on the tour that followed in early 1991. “Tactical Neural Implant” (1992) turned toward more melodic, multi-layered arrangements and the heavy film sampling that became a fixture of the sound. Five remixes for Fear Factory’s “Fear Is the Mindkiller” EP in 1993 fed directly into “Millennium” (1994), the band’s first industrial metal record, built on metal guitar samples and Devin Townsend’s session work. “Hard Wired” arrived the following September. Fulber left in 1997 to concentrate on production, and Peterson took his place for “FLAvour of the Weak” (1997), “Implode” (1999) and “Epitaph” (2001), a run that traded the metal influences for breakbeat and big beat. Fulber returned for “Civilization” (2004), and Peterson rejoined for “Artificial Soldier” (2006), the first album to feature Jeremy Inkel and Jared Slingerland. “Improvised Electronic Device” (2010), “Echogenetic” (2013), “Wake Up the Coma” (2019) and “Mechanical Soul” (2021) followed, the last on Metropolis. The band also composed soundtracks for the games “Quake III: Team Arena,” “AirMech” and “WarMech.” Inkel died on 23 January 2018 at the age of 34, from complications of an asthma condition. Leeb has run Delerium since 1987 and Noise Unit since the late 1980s, while Fulber started Conjure One after his 1997 departure and has worked with Fear Factory for decades; Side-Line published a Front Line Assembly interview – Catching up with Bill Leeb and Rhys Fulber in 2024. “Hard Wired” turns 31 this year, the record that closed out the guitar-driven stretch the band opened with “Millennium” before the electronics took over again.
items._cn_summary: Front Line Assembly 第八张录音室专辑《Hard Wired》于1995年9月发行，由Bill Leeb与Rhys Fulber联手制作并包揽全部十首曲目的创作。专辑长达62分钟，融合电子工业与暗潮的冷硬质感，邀请Devin Townsend担任电吉他客串，Dave McKean负责视觉设计。制作采用先曲后词的工作流程，歌词聚焦于人类与技术的对抗——技术既在毁灭地球又是拯救的唯一途径，这一矛盾贯穿于大量电影采样中。制作人Greg Reely延续自1990年《Caustic Grip》以来的合作关系，整张专辑在Warehouse工作室耗时约五个月完成。唯一单曲《Circuitry》限量版以双CD形式发行，收录Haujobb与Biosphere的混音作品以及两首非专辑曲目。专辑在瑞典取得第47名并售出至少五万张。整体内容偏向背景信息梳理而非深度评论。

Ghosts In The Graveyard return to their 2016 debut, Monsters For The Masses, with the zeal of directors who finally found the budget they wanted the first time around.
